articles.title: Suspected Chinese Agents Are Trying to Dupe Americans with Fake Listings on Job Platforms
articles.body:
Suspected Chinese Agents Are Trying to Dupe Americans with Fake Listings on Job Platforms (cnn.com) 17
			
		 	
				"LinkedIn is probably the greatest intelligence tool that's ever been created," CNN heard from Holden Triplett, director of counterintelligence at the National Security Council in the first Trump administration.
A LinkedIn spokesperson responded that "Creating a fake account or misrepresenting your identity is a clear violation of our terms of service."  (And they also told CNN that LinkedIn remains "focused on detecting state-sponsored abuse and will continue to enforce our policies against fake accounts.")  But it's not just happening on LinkedIn...
Suspected Chinese spies have created an elaborate web of fake firms with job opportunities aimed at tricking current and former US officials into divulging government secrets as part of a scheme that is more pervasive than previously reported, CNN has found.  Interviews with a dozen people caught up in the operation — as well as CNN analysis of suspected bogus websites — reveal how there is a much broader target pool for obtaining sensitive US information after the Trump administration laid off thousands of federal employees. [CNN reported in 2025 that "foreign powers such as China and Russia" had directed their intelligence services "to ramp up recruiting of Americans working in national security by targeting those who had been fired or felt they were at risk of losing their jobs".] These workers left their posts with inadequate guidance and protection from spying plots, ex-officials said, creating a potentially valuable resource for Beijing and weak spot for Washington...  In addition to government workers, the plot has targeted journalists, trade consultants and others, who might have knowledge deemed valuable to US adversaries.
The FBI offered a glimpse into the malicious recruiting scam when it seized 13 websites officials say were tied to fake consulting firms in June. China denied the FBI allegations. CNN analyzed the sites' software code, looked at other suspicious job listings, and interviewed people approached by similar companies. CNN identified several more websites that mimicked the style and substance of those disabled by the FBI.   Two more sites that Max Lesser, a senior analyst at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies think tank, discovered and shared with CNN have some of the same web infrastructure or other connections to the seized websites.  In total, Lesser has uncovered more than 100 other web domains, many of which share similar characteristics with the sites taken down by the FBI....
This sprawling network has the hallmarks of a Chinese intelligence operation, Lesser told CNN.  
After creating fake web sites, the operatives "plant vague, well-paying job ads for consulting positions focused on China-related issues" on jobs sites like LinkedIn, CNN reports, asking applicants to produce "research reports". ("[D]ozens or hundreds of such reports, across various topics of interest to Beijing, can start to form a much clearer picture of US national security policy and its vulnerabilities, according to current and former FBI officials.")
CNN sent a detailed request for a comment to a spokesperson for the Chinese embassy in Washington, DC.  "I am not familiar with what you mentioned," they responded, adding that China "opposes vilifying China by peddling the so-called 'Chinese spy' narrative."

articles.title: SpaceX Wins FCC Approval To Deploy 1 Million Orbital Data Center Satellites
articles.body:
SpaceX Wins FCC Approval To Deploy 1 Million Orbital Data Center Satellites 101
			
		 	
				The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has authorized SpaceX to deploy one million AI computing satellites into orbit as part of its solar-powered Starmind data center constellation. The approval comes despite opposition from Amazon, Viasat and the American Astronomical Society. CNBC reports:  The FCC, in its authorization filing (PDF), noted that SpaceX's application "received a substantial number of comments from the public, including petitions to deny filed by Kuiper Systems LLC (Amazon Leo), Viasat Inc. (Viasat), and the American Astronomical Society (AAS)." In a March petition urging the FCC to deny SpaceX's application, Amazon had labeled the company's Starmind project as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan."
The e-commerce and cloud computing giant is building a competitor to SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, and said it would take SpaceX "centuries" to build the constellation, adding that the company provided scant details about how it would "deliver on these grand claims." The petition resulted in a rebuke from [FCC Chairman Brendan Carr], who said Amazon "should focus on the fact" that it's falling short of its own satellite deployment milestone.  In a post on X, Carr said SpaceX's Starmind constellation and "competitor constellations will use solar power to extend America's lead in Super Intelligence."
Musk said in a reply, "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."

articles.title: SpaceX wins FCC approval to deploy 1M orbital data center satellites
articles.body:
The Federal Communications Commission has authorized Elon Musk's SpaceX to put 1 million artificial intelligence computing satellites in orbit, Chairman Brendan Carr announced on Wednesday.
Carr said in a post on X, the social network owned by SpaceX, that the company's Starmind constellation, and "competitor constellations will use solar power to extend America's lead" in AI.
Musk said in a reply, "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."
The FCC, in its authorization filing, noted that SpaceX's application "received a substantial number of comments from the public, including petitions to deny filed by Kuiper Systems LLC (Amazon Leo), Viasat Inc. (Viasat), and the American Astronomical Society (AAS)."
In a March petition urging the FCC to deny SpaceX's application, Amazon had labeled the company's Starmind project as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan."
The e-commerce and cloud computing giant is building a competitor to SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, and said it would take SpaceX "centuries" to build the constellation, adding that the company provided scant details about how it would "deliver on these grand claims."
The petition resulted in a rebuke from Carr, who said Amazon "should focus on the fact" that it's falling short of its own satellite deployment milestone.
Amazon declined to comment on the FCC's approval.
Other companies have also set their sights on orbital data centers. Google last year announced Project Suncatcher, which it describes as a "moonshot to put AI in space," and launched its first chips into space on a SpaceX rocket and Planet Labs satellite in October.
In March, Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin petitioned the FCC to let it launch up to 51,600 satellites as part of a low Earth orbit satellite constellation dubbed "Project Sunrise." The constellation would work in tandem with Blue Origin's planned TeraWave satellite internet service, announced in January.
Astrophysicist and author Adam Becker was critical of the FCC move in an email to CNBC on Wednesday.
"Any serious attempt at this is going to further pollute the night sky and runs a serious risk of a cascading chain reaction of space junk collisions, which would be a disaster for all of humanity," he wrote. "Musk and Carr are either profoundly stupid themselves, or hoping the rest of us are too stupid to notice this is nonsense."
SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.
A senior attorney with Earthjustice, Jan Hasselman, criticized the FCC for issuing its decision on a holiday week, and approving the SpaceX proposal without any environmental review, which he said was required by the National Environmental Policy Act.
The FCC said in its authorization that it dismissed "comments and concerns raised regarding topics over which the Commission has no authority, including environmental concerns," and concerns about its impact on "optical astronomy."

articles.title: The Big Idea: Alma Alexander
articles.body:
The Big Idea: Alma Alexander
Posted on November 25, 2026 Posted by Athena Scalzi 2 Comments
Real life mythos and legends often play a role in creating a fantasy world 0f one’s own, and author Alma Alexander has an especially unique myth0logy (one that is personal to her) that she is drawing from for the first book in her new trilogy, The Shadow Before the Dawn.
ALMA ALEXANDER:
Back in the 12th century, a quondam poet wrote an epic that contained the line, “There are only three subject matters for any discerning man: that of France, that of Britain, and that of Great Rome.” Possibly the most immediately familiar one of these would be the Matter of Britain – you will know it as the body of medieval literature associated with Great and with Less Britain (Brittany, for those who recognize it better by that name), and concerned with the legendary kings and heroes associated with it, King Arthur, Lancelot, the Knights of the Round Table, the Holy Grail, all that (mostly, blame Geoffrey of Monmouth). The Matter of France deals with Charlemagne and his paladins, and their wars with Moors and Saracens. The Matter of Rome, or Res Romana, is a more rarefied elixir of Greek and Roman mythology, which includes the Matter of Troy (hence the Odyssey and the Iliad), and which focused on military heroes like Alexander the Great and Julius Caesar.
But although those three were “anointed”, as it were, there are very much other “Matters” out there, for various countries and cultures. We might argue about whether Wagner muddied the waters with the Ring of the Nibelungen and twisted Matters of Norse origin and of German origin together in a Gordian knot; the Matter of Spain could be – well – maybe El Cid (Spanish people, feel free to correct me); we might definitely argue about the Matter of America, and about ideas it might contain, such as Manifest Destiny. The Matters of Countries are the invisible backbones upon which the shape of their existence hangs.
There is a Matter hidden deep in Eastern Europe, my own Matter, which talks of a line of Kings who walked into being a line of Saints, who created a kingdom out of a smattering of feeble little fiefdoms, and then forged it into an empire, and then fought a Last Battle in which everything they wrought in the Earthly realm was destroyed but which wrote their lineage into the Heavenly ledgers forever and gave their people the light they needed in order to survive the 500 years of slavery that followed their loss in that Last Battle. I am talking about the Nemanjic Dynasty in the 12th/13th centuries Balkans.
For a long time I have wanted to go back to that ancient tree and pick its fruit. This is my own Matter, the one that belongs to my own background, to my own people. It is a period stuffed with history, mystery, miracles, myths, legends, and larger-than-life characters, ripe for the plucking, and one which is rather less well known to the English-language reading public than the more easily accessible Matters out there. I started on a version of this story years ago, and wrote about 20,000 words of it, and then Life fell on me like a landslide and I lost in quick succession my husband, my mother, and a 19-year-old cat (don’t just dismiss this last; I had raised her from a 9-week-old kitten who weighed less than what it would take to make a decent hamburger when she came into my hands, and her loss HURT).
For six years I was a caregiver and then (in increasingly dense layers) someone who mourned and grieved, and all of that leaves little room for telling stories… so I kind of stopped writing. At all. And then, somehow, I picked up those twenty thousand words and looked at them again. And realized that I needed to tell another story before the story that I set out to tell in the first place. And then I realized that I needed to tell another story before THAT, to give weight and stability to the Matter I was addressing. And just like that, I had a trilogy on my hands.
The Shadow Before the Dawn, book 1 in what became that trilogy, was finally fully formed in 2026. The other books are in process. But that first book… this story matters to me, right from that beginning, deeply, organically. Sometimes I think everything I have ever written was training for this story, these books, to which I feel a true responsibility and which I am dedicated to giving the respect and dignity that they deserve.
Because I am writing a Matter. A story that shaped a nation.
You might not know this story.
Come with me, and let me open the doors into a world full of a magic which may be rich and strange and unfamiliar to you. It isn’t to me. This is my Matter, and it runs in my blood. I hope, when you are done reading this, that you will judge that I have done justice to it.
The Shadow Before the Dawn: Amazon

articles.title: Bare Metal Qwen
articles.body:
A standalone bootable x86-64 operating system that runs Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B directly on hardware or KVM with no Linux, no Windows, no C, no Rust, and no libc.
- 24,252 bytes stripped static Multiboot 1 kernel (FAST_Q8=1, default: .text = 17,143 B, .rodata = 2,772 B, .bss = 2.1 MiB NOBITS, zero dynamic dependencies), or 23,612 bytes (FAST_Q8=0, legacy Q8_0xFP32).
- 74–94 ms cold boot to interactive asm-llm> multi-turn chat with persistent KV-cache across turns, all SMP cores online, and the .asmbin v2 (614 MiB FP16 scales) or v1 (649 MiB FP32 scales) model bound zero-copy from physical RAM on 2 MiB huge pages.
- 100% token-exact and byte-for-byte parity with Phase 1 across 1..32 vCPUs.
- 134.9 tok/s decode on QEMU KVM (AMD EPYC 7642, 16 vCPUs; 23.7 tok/s at 1 vCPU, 118.1 tok/s at 8 vCPUs, 136.6 tok/s peak) and 55.4 tok/s live on a 0 GB disk Proxmox VE VM (Intel Xeon E5-2670 v3, 12 cores).
Running live on a diskless (0 GB storage) Proxmox VE VM booted from the hybrid BIOS+UEFI ISO (Intel Xeon E5-2670 v3, 12 cores, 2 GiB RAM):
- x86-64 CPU with AVX2 + FMA + F16C.
- Core build & QEMU KVM:
sudo apt install nasm binutils qemu-system-x86
- Optional, for building a bootable BIOS+UEFI hybrid ISO (make os-iso): sudo apt install grub-pc-bin grub-efi-amd64-bin grub-common mtools xorriso
- An exported models/qwen3-0.6b-q8_0.asmbin file (--scale-dtype fp16 v2 recommended, or legacy v1 --scale-dtype fp32; see Phase 1 setup).
From the repository root (FAST_Q8=1 is enabled by default; pass FAST_Q8=0 for legacy FP32-activation mode):
make os FAST_Q8=1
make os-check
Expected output (FAST_Q8=1):
-rwxr-xr-x 1 user user 24252 build/asm-llm-os.elf
build/asm-llm-os.elf: ELF 32-bit LSB executable, Intel 80386, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
There is no dynamic section in this file.
(The kernel is linked as 64-bit ELF and wrapped into ELF32 via objcopy -O elf32-i386 for standard Multiboot 1 loaders like QEMU -kernel and GRUB2; boot.asm transitions immediately into 64-bit Long Mode.)
Boot directly in the terminal over COM1 serial (-nographic):
qemu-system-x86_64 -enable-kvm -cpu host -m 2G -smp 16 \
  -kernel build/asm-llm-os.elf \
  -initrd models/qwen3-0.6b-q8_0.asmbin \
  -nographic
Or use the Makefile shortcut:
make os-run MODEL=models/qwen3-0.6b-q8_0.asmbin SMP=16
Run a one-shot batch prompt with clean ACPI shutdown:
make os-run MODEL=models/qwen3-0.6b-q8_0.asmbin SMP=16 \
  CMDLINE='prompt="Explain how a CPU cache works in 3 concise sentences." max_tokens=64 think=0 shutdown=1'
Open a live 80x25 VGA GUI window with PS/2 keyboard input:
qemu-system-x86_64 -enable-kvm -cpu host -m 2G -smp 16 \
  -kernel build/asm-llm-os.elf \
  -initrd models/qwen3-0.6b-q8_0.asmbin \
  -vga std -serial stdio
Packages the 23 KB kernel, GRUB2 Multiboot 1 config, and the 649 MiB .asmbin model into a single self-contained ~661 MiB bootable ISO (build/asm-llm-os.iso):
make os-iso MODEL=models/qwen3-0.6b-q8_0.asmbin
Boot the ISO in QEMU KVM (SeaBIOS or UEFI OVMF):
# Legacy BIOS (SeaBIOS)
qemu-system-x86_64 -enable-kvm -cpu host -m 2G -smp 16 \
  -cdrom build/asm-llm-os.iso -nographic
# UEFI (OVMF)
qemu-system-x86_64 -enable-kvm -cpu host -m 2G -smp 16 \
  -bios /usr/share/ovmf/OVMF.fd \
  -cdrom build/asm-llm-os.iso -nographic
Because the entire OS and model live inside the ISO and run out of RAM, the VM needs zero hard disks.
- Upload build/asm-llm-os.iso to your Proxmox node's ISO storage (local -> ISO Images -> Upload, or scp into /var/lib/vz/template/iso/asm-llm-os.iso).
- Create and start a diskless VM on the Proxmox host (pick an unused <vmid>, e.g. 250):
qm create 250 \
  --name asm-llm-os \
  --machine pc \
  --bios seabios \
  --cpu host \
  --cores 12 \
  --memory 2048 \
  --balloon 0 \
  --vga std \
  --serial0 socket \
  --ide2 local:iso/asm-llm-os.iso,media=cdrom \
  --boot order=ide2
qm start 250
- Interact either through the Proxmox web UI (noVNC Console, VGA + PS/2 keyboard) or over the virtual serial port:
qm terminal 250
(Note: --cpu host is required so the VM exposes AVX2 + FMA, and --balloon 0 ensures 2 GiB of contiguous guest RAM for the 649 MiB model + 449 MiB KV-cache arena.)
By default, the bare-metal console runs in multi-turn chat mode with persistent KV-cache: each new user turn prefills only the new Qwen3 chat tokens starting at g_chat_pos without recomputing earlier turns, closes every assistant turn in the KV-cache with <|im_end|>\n, and displays live context usage (ctx=X/2048) in the decode stats line. When the KV-cache approaches max_seq (pos + n_prompt + 64 >= max_seq), it prints [chat] context full, resetting KV-cache and resets cleanly. If booted with prompt="..." and shutdown=0, the initial batch turn stays in the KV-cache so you can continue the same conversation in the REPL.
Both PS/2 keyboard (VGA) and COM1 serial (115200 8N1) are polled simultaneously. Type any message and press Enter, or use a built-in command:
Pass via QEMU -append "...", make os-run CMDLINE='...', or make os-iso CMDLINE='...':
Phase 2 compiles the exact same shared/math.asm, shared/matmul.asm, shared/tokenizer.asm, and shared/transformer.asm with -DBARE_METAL -DFAST_Q8=$(FAST_Q8) and pairs them with 4,167 lines of bare-metal OS code:
- Boot & Long Mode (boot.asm, linker.ld): verifies Multiboot 1 magic (0x2BADB002), zeroes .bss, builds 4-level 2 MiB huge-page identity tables covering 0..4 GiB (with 0xFE000000..0xFFFFFFFF marked Strong Uncacheable for Local APIC MMIO), enters 64-bit Long Mode, installs a 32-entry exception IDT, verifies XSAVE + AVX + AVX2 + FMA + F16C via CPUID, and initializes CR0/CR4/XCR0=7/MXCSR.
- Zero-Copy Weights & Physical Arena (runtime.asm): binds the .asmbin (v2 FP16 scales or v1 FP32 scales) Multiboot module directly at its physical address (validating "ASML" magic) and carves the 449 MiB KV-cache + scratch arena from the largest usable Multiboot memory-map region, zeroing it with AVX2.

- 100% token-exact and byte-for-byte parity with Phase 1 across 1..32 vCPUs.
- 134.9 tok/s decode on QEMU KVM (AMD EPYC 7642, 16 vCPUs; 23.7 tok/s at 1 vCPU, 118.1 tok/s at 8 vCPUs, 136.6 tok/s peak) and 55.4 tok/s live on a 0 GB disk Proxmox VE VM (Intel Xeon E5-2670 v3, 12 cores).

make os FAST_Q8=1
make os-check

-rwxr-xr-x 1 user user 24252 build/asm-llm-os.elf
build/asm-llm-os.elf: ELF 32-bit LSB executable, Intel 80386, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped
There is no dynamic section in this file.
(The kernel is linked as 64-bit ELF and wrapped into ELF32 via objcopy -O elf32-i386 for standard Multiboot 1 loaders like QEMU -kernel and GRUB2; boot.asm transitions immediately into 64-bit Long Mode.)

  -kernel build/asm-llm-os.elf \
  -initrd models/qwen3-0.6b-q8_0.asmbin \
  -nographic

make os-run MODEL=models/qwen3-0.6b-q8_0.asmbin SMP=16

make os-run MODEL=models/qwen3-0.6b-q8_0.asmbin SMP=16 \

  -kernel build/asm-llm-os.elf \
  -initrd models/qwen3-0.6b-q8_0.asmbin \
  -vga std -serial stdio
Packages the 23 KB kernel, GRUB2 Multiboot 1 config, and the 649 MiB .asmbin model into a single self-contained ~661 MiB bootable ISO (build/asm-llm-os.iso):
make os-iso MODEL=models/qwen3-0.6b-q8_0.asmbin

qemu-system-x86_64 -enable-kvm -cpu host -m 2G -smp 16 \
  -cdrom build/asm-llm-os.iso -nographic
# UEFI (OVMF)
qemu-system-x86_64 -enable-kvm -cpu host -m 2G -smp 16 \
  -bios /usr/share/ovmf/OVMF.fd \

articles.title: EPA reports ‘zero’ airborne lead following controlled Army detonation in Iowa
articles.body:
Saying it was necessary to prevent the possible spontaneous explosion of a stockpile of material used in igniters and blasting caps, the US Army conducted a controlled detonation of over 9,700 pounds of lead azide today at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, Iowa. Videos of the detonation showed plumes of smoke several hundred feet high drifting south before quickly dissipating.
EPA reports ‘zero’ airborne lead following controlled Army detonation in Iowa
Hours after detonating 4.4 tons of lead azide in Iowa, officials reported early test results from the surrounding areas.
Following the explosion, the Army confirmed that all of the barrels at the plant had been destroyed without any secondary explosions or infrastructure damage. “I believe, absolutely, that we reduced, as close to zero as it’s absolutely humanly possible, the risk to the health and safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa,” said Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley during a press conference held two hours after the blast, according to the Associated Press.
The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has been monitoring the area around the ammunition plant leading up to today’s event. According to a statement from the EPA following the detonation, “real-time air monitors are reporting zero detection of airborne lead throughout the region” an hour after the detonation. The data collected by EPA employees, contractors, and monitoring equipment is shared here.
The Army has used lead azide in munitions for nearly a century but began transitioning away from the material around 15 years ago because it can be difficult to transport and store. Over time, the material can degrade and crystallize and eventually become unstable enough to detonate at ambient temperatures. The Iowa ammunition plant housed 68 barrels containing about 9,700 pounds of lead azide, representing the country’s remaining stockpile. For safety reasons, the material was stored in liquid form embedded in sawdust and burlap bags while water and ethanol were added to prevent freezing. However, the decision was made to detonate the stockpile after an inspection by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms (ATF) discovered “significant crystallization on the exterior of the barrels” last March.
Ahead of today’s detonation, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) supported a recommended, but voluntary, temporary relocation of all the residents of Middletown and immediate surrounding areas that began yesterday. A cone-shaped evacuation zone extends about five miles southwest of the ammunition plant to account for the post-explosion dispersion and deposition path of dust. Displaced residents will be lodged until Friday, November 27th, and can return home once the all-clear has been given.
To reduce the amount of lead dust released into surrounding areas and the environment, the Army said it took several additional precautions as part of today’s detonation. Walls made of four 16,000-gallon water tanks were installed to capture lead particulate, while the aging earth-covered magazines holding the barrels were covered with tarps and lead containment screens and flooded with foam.

articles.title: Disney Plus, Hulu, and HBO Max are all over 50 percent off for Black Friday
articles.body:
Black Friday isn’t just a good time to save on a new TV but also a chance to spend less on what you watch on it. The shopping holiday often brings steep streaming discounts, and this year is no exception, with some streamers offering more than 50 percent off. HBO Max, Apple TV, and Hulu are all offering deals, with several plans going for just a few dollars a month. Some discounts even apply to ad-free plans, though there are fewer than last year and prices are generally higher.
Disney Plus, Hulu, and HBO Max are all over 50 percent off for Black Friday
Many services are offering discounts that last anywhere from two months to a full year.
Still, you can save big if you don’t mind a few commercials. Right now, for example, you can get a year of the ad-supported Disney Plus and Hulu bundle for $4.99 a month, saving you $96, or sign up for the most basic HBO Max plan for $5.49 a month for 12 months, saving you $66. We’ve rounded up these deals and more below, including what each plan offers and how long you can take advantage of the discounted rate.
Disney Plus and Hulu
With everything from Disney classics and Marvel movies to FX dramas like The Bear and Shōgun, the Disney Plus and Hulu bundle offers plenty for the whole family to watch. For Black Friday, you can get both services with ads for just $4.99 per month ($8 off) for a year via Hulu or Disney Plus, saving you $96 in total. The ad-free bundle is also on sale for $14.99 per month ($7 off) for 12 months, saving you $84. Both discounts are available through 11:59PM PT on November 30th.
Whichever plan you choose, you’ll get access to both streaming libraries. Hulu offers dramas like Furious, Alien: Earth, The Lowdown, and The Handmaid’s Tale, as well as comedies like Bob’s Burgers, Futurama, and It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia. Disney Plus, meanwhile, is home to Disney and Pixar favorites, The Simpsons, and a wide selection of Star Wars and Marvel movies and shows. It’s also a good option for holiday movie nights, with classics like Home Alone and The Santa Clause.
HBO Max
HBO Max is home to some of Hollywood’s biggest releases, and right now, you can watch them for half the usual rate. Now through November 30th, new and returning subscribers can sign up for HBO Max’s Basic With Ads plan for $5.49 a month via HBO Max or Amazon, saving you $66 over the course of a year.
Although the plan doesn’t include live sports, it supports simultaneous streaming on two devices and gives you access to everything from award-winning films like Sinners and Marty Supreme to Wuthering Heights. There’s arguably even more to watch on the TV front, from dramas like The Gilded Age, Lanterns, Euphoria, and Heated Rivalry to comedies such as Hacks and The Righteous Gemstones. Fantasy fans, meanwhile, can immerse themselves in the world of Game of Thrones and its spinoffs, including House of the Dragon and A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, or check out Dune: Prophecy. You’ll also be able to stream new releases, including HBO’s upcoming Harry Potter series.
Peacock
If you’re looking for an affordable way to catch up on NBC shows, Peacock’s Black Friday promotion offers two ways to save. Through November 30th, new and returning subscribers can sign up for Peacock Select for $2.99 a month ($6 off) for three months or $29.99 ($60 off) for a full year. For access to Peacock’s larger catalog, you can also subscribe to Peacock Premium for $8.99 per month for three months or $89.99 ($40 off) for a year.
The cheaper Select tier is a particularly good value if you mainly watch shows from networks like NBC, Bravo, and Telemundo, including Saturday Night Live, The Office, and Below Deck. Movie buffs and sports fans, however, will prefer Premium, which offers access to a much wider selection of entertainment. Peacock’s catalog includes films like The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, Disclosure Day, and Minions & Monsters, along with shows like The Good Daughter, Dig, and The Paper. A Premium subscription also lets you watch live sporting events, including Sunday Night Football, as well as Peacock originals, such as the various Love Island spinoffs.
Paramount Plus
If you’re a Star Trek fan or want another way to watch live sports, Paramount Plus is down to $2.99 per month for two months for Black Friday. New and eligible returning subscribers can take advantage of the discount through November 30th, bringing the cost of both the Essential and Premium plans to $5.98 for the introductory period. That makes Premium a particularly good deal, since it normally costs $13.99 a month, compared to $8.99 for the ad-supported Essential tier.
Paramount Plus includes CBS shows like NCIS and Everybody Loves Raymond to Tulsa King and the various Yellowstone spinoffs, including both 1883 and 1923. Movie fans can also browse Paramount’s film library, which includes titles like Arrival, Top Gun, and Interstellar, while sports fans can watch select NFL games, UFC events, UEFA Champions League matches, and March Madness games. Premium also grants you access to Showtime originals and a live feed of your local CBS station, along with ad-free on-demand viewing, though live programming still includes commercials.
Apple TV
Apple TV has built an impressive collection of acclaimed shows, particularly if you’re into sci-fi shows like Silo or thrillers like Slow Horses. Right now, US customers with an Amazon account can subscribe to Apple TV through Amazon for $6.99 per month ($8 off) for six months, saving $48 over the introductory period. Amazon hasn’t listed an end date for the promotion, either.
Six months should give you plenty of time to work through Apple’s other originals, including Severance, Pachinko, The Morning Show, and Pluribus, or settle in for a movie like Arrival or Anchorman. The service also includes live sports, specifically Formula 1 races and Major League Soccer matches.
Crunchyroll
Anime fans can spend the next six months catching up on shows like The Apothecary Diaries, Jujutsu Kaisen, Black Clover, and One Piece for a lot less thanks to Crunchyroll’s Black Friday sale. Select new and returning subscribers in the US can sign up for the Fan plan for $3.99 a month ($6 off) for six months, saving them $36. The Mega Fan tier is also down to $5.99 a month ($8 off) for six months, while Ultimate Fan is available for $8.99 a month ($9 off) for the same period. Amazon is also offering the same discount on the Mega Fan tier.
All three subscriptions offer access to Crunchyroll’s full anime library without ads, including new episodes shortly after they air in Japan. The Fan tier lets you watch on one device at a time, while Mega Fan increases that limit to four devices and adds offline viewing and access to Crunchyroll’s Game Vault. Ultimate Fan, meanwhile, supports six simultaneous streams and includes Crunchyroll Manga, along with additional store perks.
Starz
If you didn’t get a chance to watch the Michael Jackson biopic Michael when it was released earlier this year or just want to catch up on Outlander, Starz is offering a particularly affordable way to stream both on Black Friday. Eligible subscribers can sign up for a year directly through Starz or Amazon Prime for $11.99 ($58 off), which works out to about $1 a month when you pay upfront. If you’d rather not commit to a year, you can alternatively subscribe for $2.99 per month ($9 off) for three months. Either option lets you explore Starz’s catalog of films and TV shows, including In the Grey, Power Ballad, Splash City, and P-Valley.
Other streaming deals of note
Amazon is also discounting a wide range of subscriptions through Prime Video, including NBA League Pass, AMC Plus, MGM Plus, and several bundles. Most of the deals below are available through November 30th.

You can also get AMC Plus, MGM Plus, and Starz together for $5.49 per month (about $16 off) for two months.

articles.title: S&P Warns Nvidia's Board May Be Compromised
articles.body:
S&P Warns Nvidia's Board May Be Compromised (usnews.com)
			
		 	
				S&P Global Ratings has placed Nvidia's AA credit rating on downgrade watch, warning that Jensen Huang's departure and subsequent reinstatement as CEO exposed weaknesses in the company's corporate governance and board oversight. "We believe the long tenure of certain board members may have compromised their independence. The company's corporate governance practices may also not have kept pace with Nvidia's rapid growth and its role as a critical global technology enabler," the ratings agency said. Reuters reports:  Nvidia currently has an 'AA' rating from S&P, which indicates a very strong capacity to meet financial commitments. The highest rating is 'AAA'. The agency said it could downgrade Nvidia within the next 90 days, but expects any potential downgrade to be limited to one notch, unless investigations and other disclosures harm the company's reputation or future business prospects. Meanwhile, Moody's said on Wednesday that bringing back Huang eases near-term uncertainty around Nvidia's business execution and eliminates execution risk associated with appointing a new leader for the chipmaker. The agency said Nvidia's Aa1 rating and stable outlook remain unaffected, but added that governance and regulatory uncertainty persists.

articles.title: Euro-Office comes to your desktop with the Nextcloud Office Desktop app
articles.body:
On June 9, 2026, we released the first production-ready version of Euro-Office, a sovereign collaborative office suite developed and governed in Europe. With Nextcloud Hub 26 Summer, we announced the release of the Nextcloud Office Desktop app powered by Euro-Office. Today, the ready-to-use version of the app is available for download. It lets you work offline, switch between Nextcloud Hub in your browser and the app on your computer, and get the same experience on Windows, macOS and Linux.
In this article, you’ll learn about the app’s features, how to install it on Windows, macOS and Linux, and how to co-edit files with your team through Nextcloud Hub.
Free desktop office with maximum file compatibility
The Nextcloud Office Desktop app is a free and open source office suite for Windows, macOS and Linux. Featuring editors for text documents, spreadsheets, presentations, and PDFs, it offers high compatibility with Microsoft Office formats (DOCX, XLSX, PPTX) and open formats (ODT, ODS, ODP). Connect it to Nextcloud Hub to edit files with your team in real time.
The app includes the features of Nextcloud Office in your browser, plus the benefits of working on your computer:
- Work offline and keep files on your device
- Use the fonts installed on your computer
- Sign documents digitally
Work with local and online files
With the Nextcloud Office Desktop app, you can edit files locally without an internet connection. Working locally, you keep access to your files and you can keep working when you don’t have internet connection or your online tools go down. You decide which files stay on your computer and which go to the cloud.
Need to access your online files? You can connect your Nextcloud instance to the Nextcloud Office Desktop app to access all the files available to you, and edit them on your own or with your team in real time.
How to connect the Nextcloud Office Desktop app to the cloud:
- Click “+” in the “Clouds” section in the Home tab
- Choose “Nextcloud“ and specify the URL of your instance
- Log in with your credentials
Once connected, choose your Nextcloud instance from the list. You can connect more than one instance to one app to have access to multiple cloud working environments.
Use your own fonts
The Nextcloud Office Desktop app uses fonts installed on your machine, including corporate fonts and default fonts from your OS, like Microsoft fonts on Windows. You can install additional custom fonts any time. No need to bother your Nextcloud admins!
Note: if your collaborators don’t have the same font, they’ll see a fallback font in their version of the file.
Digital signatures and file protection
The Nextcloud Office Desktop app lets you use digital signatures to sign your documents, spreadsheets and presentations. A signature shows who signed a file and that nobody has changed it since. Go to Protection tab and add a signature via Signature feature.
Keep in mind that you need a digital certificate to sign documents. To obtain one, you can ask your IT team at work, or get one for personal use from a trusted provider. You can find providers approved in the EU in this list.
In the Protection tab, you can also set a password for a file, or limit what others can do: comment, fill in forms, or edit with tracked changes only.
How to install the Euro-Office desktop app
You can find and download the latest version of the Nextcloud Office Desktop app from our official installation page.
The app is available for:
- Windows: x64, ARM64
- Linux: .deb (Debian, Ubuntu), .rpm (Fedora)
- macOS (Apple Silicon)
You can also find unsigned builds of Euro-Office desktop app and build the app from the source yourself by following the instructions on GitHub.
We want to keep improving the app. You are welcome to share any issues you find with our engineering team on GitHub.
Want to contribute to Euro-Office? Here’s how to get involved
Contributions are welcome! Whether it’s a bug report, a feature idea, a translation, or a pull request, here’s how to take part:
- Found a bug or have an idea? Open an issue and describe what you ran into or what you’d like to see.
- Want to contribute code? Fork the relevant component repo, make your change, and open a pull request. For build changes, see the build docs.
- Want to help translate? Localization improvements are always appreciated — see the editors’ interface translations.
Please keep contributions compatible with the project’s AGPL v3 license.

articles.title: Euro-Office comes to your desktop with the Nextcloud Office Desktop app
articles.body:
On June 9, 2026, we released the first production-ready version of Euro-Office, a sovereign collaborative office suite developed and governed in Europe. With Nextcloud Hub 26 Summer, we announced the release of the Nextcloud Office Desktop app powered by Euro-Office. Today, the ready-to-use version of the app is available for download. It lets you work offline, switch between Nextcloud Hub in your browser and the app on your computer, and get the same experience on Windows, macOS and Linux.
In this article, you’ll learn about the app’s features, how to install it on Windows, macOS and Linux, and how to co-edit files with your team through Nextcloud Hub.
Free desktop office with maximum file compatibility
The Nextcloud Office Desktop app is a free and open source office suite for Windows, macOS and Linux. Featuring editors for text documents, spreadsheets, presentations, and PDFs, it offers high compatibility with Microsoft Office formats (DOCX, XLSX, PPTX) and open formats (ODT, ODS, ODP). Connect it to Nextcloud Hub to edit files with your team in real time.
The app includes the features of Nextcloud Office in your browser, plus the benefits of working on your computer:
- Work offline and keep files on your device
- Use the fonts installed on your computer
- Sign documents digitally
Work with local and online files
With the Nextcloud Office Desktop app, you can edit files locally without an internet connection. Working locally, you keep access to your files and you can keep working when you don’t have internet connection or your online tools go down. You decide which files stay on your computer and which go to the cloud.
Need to access your online files? You can connect your Nextcloud instance to the Nextcloud Office Desktop app to access all the files available to you, and edit them on your own or with your team in real time.
How to connect the Nextcloud Office Desktop app to the cloud:
- Click “+” in the “Clouds” section in the Home tab
- Choose “Nextcloud“ and specify the URL of your instance
- Log in with your credentials
Once connected, choose your Nextcloud instance from the list. You can connect more than one instance to one app to have access to multiple cloud working environments.
Use your own fonts
The Nextcloud Office Desktop app uses fonts installed on your machine, including corporate fonts and default fonts from your OS, like Microsoft fonts on Windows. You can install additional custom fonts any time. No need to bother your Nextcloud admins!
Note: if your collaborators don’t have the same font, they’ll see a fallback font in their version of the file.
Digital signatures and file protection
The Nextcloud Office Desktop app lets you use digital signatures to sign your documents, spreadsheets and presentations. A signature shows who signed a file and that nobody has changed it since. Go to Protection tab and add a signature via Signature feature.
Keep in mind that you need a digital certificate to sign documents. To obtain one, you can ask your IT team at work, or get one for personal use from a trusted provider. You can find providers approved in the EU in this list.
In the Protection tab, you can also set a password for a file, or limit what others can do: comment, fill in forms, or edit with tracked changes only.
How to install the Euro-Office desktop app
You can find and download the latest version of the Nextcloud Office Desktop app from our official installation page.
The app is available for:
- Windows: x64, ARM64
- Linux: .deb (Debian, Ubuntu), .rpm (Fedora)
- macOS (Apple Silicon)
You can also find unsigned builds of Euro-Office desktop app and build the app from the source yourself by following the instructions on GitHub.
We want to keep improving the app. You are welcome to share any issues you find with our engineering team on GitHub.
Want to contribute to Euro-Office? Here’s how to get involved
Contributions are welcome! Whether it’s a bug report, a feature idea, a translation, or a pull request, here’s how to take part:
- Found a bug or have an idea? Open an issue and describe what you ran into or what you’d like to see.
- Want to contribute code? Fork the relevant component repo, make your change, and open a pull request. For build changes, see the build docs.
- Want to help translate? Localization improvements are always appreciated — see the editors’ interface translations.
Please keep contributions compatible with the project’s AGPL v3 license.

articles.title: An algebraic quantization of gravity from the null cone
articles.body:
High Energy Physics - Theory
  [Submitted on 25 Nov 2026]
Title:An algebraic quantization of gravity from the null cone
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:We propose a background independent quantization of vacuum general relativity on four dimensional Lorentzian spacetimes. Starting from first order gravity, we solve the gravitational constraints on intersecting null cones of a bulk subregion and obtain the reduced phase space at finite $G_N$. We promote its canonical Poisson brackets to commutation relations and use deformations of the reduced action to define an algebra of observables. Equipped with this, we use Gaussian wavefunctions of canonical pairs to construct a nonperturbative Hilbert space representation, for which this algebra generates a type I factor. By composing amplitudes between states prepared on null cones, we then obtain a Lorentzian path integral in which each sum over intermediate states converges absolutely. As a check, we compute the amplitude for graviton pair creation and annihilation on a null cone nonperturbatively in $G_N$ and find a finite closed form expression, even though expanding first in $G_N$ yields a logarithmic divergence. We next use diffeomorphism invariance of the path integral to show that a macroscopic causal diamond with a given maximum size has a finite dimensional Hilbert space. From the Lorentzian trace we obtain the Bekenstein Hawking entropy for marginally trapped surfaces and calculate its logarithmic correction for large Schwarzschild black holes, recovering at one loop the coefficient Sen obtained through Euclidean methods. We end by deriving the semiclassical Einstein equations to one loop as the low energy limit of this theory.

articles.title: Qualcomm's Oryon 3 Reaches the Top
articles.body:
Qualcomm’s laptop effort had humble beginnings. Their early Arm-based laptops used cell phone SoCs, and suffered from noticeably poor performance even against lower end Intel chips. But breaking into the PC market was going to be a marathon rather than a sprint, and Qualcomm has been persistent. Qualcomm created higher performance Snapdragon variants targeted at laptops, which became increasingly competent with each generation. Now, Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme can deliver CPU performance that challenges the best of its x86-64 competition. To deliver that performance, Qualcomm relies on the third generation of their in-house Oryon architecture, which I’ll call Oryon 3 for short.
The Snapdragon X2 Elite deploys Oryon 3 in both E-Core and P-Core variants, which Qualcomm confusingly calls “performance” and “prime” cores, respectively. P-Cores are the star of the show in the Snapdragon X2 Elite, where they provide both maximum single threaded performance while also providing the bulk of multithreaded throughput. That’s because Qualcomm has P-Cores outnumber their E-Cores by a factor of two, creating an inverted hybrid strategy compared to Intel’s. Thanks to this strategy, Qualcomm’s Oryon 3 P-Core variant shoulders most of the burden when it comes to Qualcomm’s PC market ambitions.
Oryon 3 takes on this burden by deploying an architecture with a strong resemblance to the first Oryon generation. Qualcomm technically has a second generation Oryon core, but only used it in phones. Their website also suggests it’s a very minor change over the first generation, so I’ll be treating first generation Oryon as Oryon 3’s direct predecessor.
Similarity to Oryon 1 is a good thing, because that gives Oryon 3 just about everything you could ask for from a 2026-era high performance design. From Oryon 1, Oryon 3 inherits an out-of-order window in excess of 600 micro-ops. Qualcomm has also carried forward a two-level cache setup that emphasizes speed over capacity. Compared to its predecessor, Oryon 3 takes things up a notch by pushing clock speeds to 5 GHz. It’s a huge 16% increase over the 4.3 GHz speed that Oryon 1 could reach, and is enough to offer a generational performance gain on its own. But Qualcomm doesn’t stop there. Oryon 3 increases core width to 9 micro-ops, up from 8 in its predecessor, and makes a number of improvements throughout the pipeline. Qualcomm brings SVE2 and SME support to the new core as well, keeping it up-to-date with the evolving aarch64 architecture and opening up new software optimization opportunities. In its role as a maximum performance architecture, Oryon 3 faces off against the likes of AMD’s Zen 5 and Intel’s Lion Cove. Arm’s Cortex X925 is another competitor, thanks to Nvidia’s laptop push with N1X.
A Faster Frontend
Setting aside clock speed, Oryon 3’s headline architectural improvement is a core width increase from 8 to 9 ups. At the frontend, Qualcomm supports this by adding another decode slot. The fetch and decode pipeline otherwise looks mostly unchanged. Oryon 1 already had over-provisioned instruction cache bandwidth at 64 bytes per cycle, which is more than sufficient to feed a 8-wide or 9-wide aarch64 decoder. Qualcomm has also kept a 192 KB, 6-way instruction cache with hardware coherency, as well as a 256 entry 8-way instruction TLB. These large structures should help the core use its fastest instruction delivery path more often than its peers, which have smaller instruction caches and instruction TLBs. Impressively, Qualcomm managed to keep these large structures and add an extra decode slot while keeping a 13 cycle branch mispredict penalty. Clock speed increases often come with compromises like longer pipelines or smaller structures, but here Qualcomm is able to have their cake and eat it too.
Testing instruction bandwidth with a stream of NOPs validates the increased decoder width when the test loop fits within the instruction cache. Improvements continue at larger instruction footprints. Oryon 3 is able to sustain about 4 NOPs/cycle from L2, compared to 2 per cycle on Oryon 1. Qualcomm might have changed something with instruction prefetching from L2, or they might have widened datapaths between the instruction cache and L2. Whatever the case, Oryon 3 now matches the likes of AMD’s Zen 5 and Intel’s Lion Coves in terms of streaming code from L2, while boasting a much larger L2. AMD and Intel’s cores do have a L3 that provides more capacity than Qualcomm’s L2, but fetching code from that L3 will cause another drop in instruction throughput.
High core throughput places pressure on the branch predictor, which must follow the instruction stream fast enough to keep the core fed. Oryon 3 improves by expanding its predecessor’s ability to handle taken branches back-to-back. Oryon 1 could only do “zero-bubble” taken branches within a 8 KB instruction footprint. Oryon 3 can do so within a 2048 branch footprint, regardless of branch spacing and code footprint. Perhaps Qualcomm switched to using a fully decoupled 2048 entry BTB. Realistically, that means Oryon 3 should be able to do zero-bubble taken branches over a branch footprint 2x to 4x larger than its predecessor, considering typical branch spacing.
Compared to AMD and Intel’s latest cores, Qualcomm lacks any ability to handle more than one taken branch per cycle. Arm’s newer cores are also capable of doing two taken branches per cycle. I suspect AMD, Arm, and Intel decided that handling multiple taken branches per cycle became more profitable once their cores got wide enough, so seeing Qualcomm build a very wide core without that ability is surprising. Perhaps clock speed factors into that decision, because going from 4.3 to 5 GHz is a huge jump. If so, Qualcomm’s choice would be justified because a clock speed increase of that magnitude probably offers a larger performance increase than going for two taken branches per cycle. Of course, it’s impossible to know if branch predictor paths presented a timing challenge for Oryon.
For branches with dynamic taken/not-taken behavior, Oryon 3 has a 2-cycle conditional predictor. Testing with branches whose outcomes correlate with increasingly long history lengths shows an average 0.5 cycle increase in time per branch over an always- taken reference run, as long as the test stays within the conditional predictor’s capabilities. Because I randomly generate patterns so that each branch is taken roughly 50% of the time, a 0.5 cycle average penalty suggests Qualcomm only incurs the 2-cycle timing if the direction predictor disagrees with a base prediction. Direction prediction starts falling apart with more than 32K patterns in play, which is an improvement over the approximately 24K patterns that first generation Oryon could handle in this test.
For comparison, Zen 5’s conditional predictor can handle roughly 48K patterns before falling apart. Unlike Oryon 3, and unlike some older Zen generations, Zen 5 does not show an increase in branch latency compared to an always-taken pattern.
Indirect branches can go to multiple targets, and present another level of difficulty because the branch predictor has to select between previously seen targets, and must store more than one target per branch. Oryon 3 has a 2-cycle indirect predictor that can track 2048 indirect targets, matching its predecessor.
A single branch can jump to 256 targets without incurring a significant penalty. This could mean at least eight of the bits that Oryon 3 uses to index into its indirect target array are influenced by branch history.
A 50 entry return stack handles return predictions, just as on Oryon 1. However, testing shows that Oryon 3 can use all 50 entries before hitting a performance degradation. When call depth exceeds return stack capacity, Oryon 3 degrades gracefully rather than immediately taking a drastic penalty as Oryon 1 does. Oryon 1’s performance drop is heavy enough to suggest it’s mispredicting every return after the return stack overflows.
Perhaps Qualcomm implemented a new mechanism to keep a single overflow from messing up the entire return stack, and lets Oryon 3 only mispredict returns whose addresses get forced out on an overflow. Whatever this optimization is, it gives Oryon 3 return prediction behavior in-line with many other cores, including AMD’s Zen 5 and Intel’s Skymont. In capacity terms, AMD’s Zen 5 has a slightly larger 52 entry return stack.
Rename/Allocate Optimizations
Optimizations at the rename and allocate stage on Qualcomm’s big core are remarkably similar to those on its little core counterpart. Both cores can eliminate up to two register-to-register MOVs per cycle. They can also eliminate up to two add-immediate instructions, as long as their immediates sum to 255 or less. It’s slightly strange that Qualcomm has kept the same optimization capability even though the big core is more than twice as wide as its little core companion. That results in degraded microbenchmark figures when I chain dependent MOVs or add-immediate instructions without a break, because the wider core can get more of those instructions into the same rename group, which means the two-per-cycle restriction causes more missed optimization opportunities.
Backend: Large, and Largely Unchanged
One of the best strategies in CPU architecture is to avoid changing something that isn’t broken. Oryon 3’s backend at a high level is basically identical to the one in its predecessor. That makes sense because if Oryon 1 encountered performance issues, they likely had little to do with its backend strategy. Qualcomm specifies a reorder buffer capacity of over 650 micro-ops for both Oryon 1 and Oryon 3. Microbenchmarking puts capacity at 675 micro-ops for Oryon 3, and 680 on Oryon 1. Register files and memory ordering queues see little to no movement in size as well.
Qualcomm’s choice to avoid major backend changes is justified, because Oryon 3’s backend structures remain competitively sized even against emerging competition like AMD’s Zen 6. Execution throughput also remains competitive. Oryon 3 does have slightly smaller memory ordering queues, and weaker vector execution throughput compared to its x86-64 counterparts. The latter comes down to having a smaller 128-bit vector width, which is especially a disadvantage against Zen 5. However, that should only affect a small minority of applications.
Even though Oryon 3’s backend is similar to its predecessor, there’s still plenty of change under the hood. Predication is a central feature in SVE2 and SME, so Oryon 3 gets a new 120 entry predicate register file. The predicate registers themselves only have to be 16 bits wide because of Oryon 3’s 128-bit vector length. But while the predicate register file doesn’t need a lot of storage, it does need to be hooked up to every major execution unit block. Predicate generation can happen from both the scalar and vector side. All four vector pipes and four load/store pipes support predication, meaning a lot of reads from the predicate register file.
New SVE2 and SME instructions also require changes to backend logic. SVE’s vector length agnostic design rides heavily on predicate generation instructions like those of the WHILE* variety (like WHILELO). Oryon 3 breaks WHILE* instructions into two micro-ops, which execute through the integer pipes to deliver a throughput of one WHILE* instruction per cycle. Predicate generation instructions that don’t require a GPR input, like PTRUE and CMPEQ, execute through two FP/vector pipes. Besides predication focused changes, SVE2 adds new math instructions like CDOT, meaning more execution unit functionality behind the vector/FP ports.
Load/Store
Like Oryon 1, Oryon 3 has a four-pipe load/store unit. Memory dependencies are handled by a robust store forwarding mechanism, which can do fast forwarding for all cases where a load overlaps a prior store. Oryon 3 is able to do that even when the load isn’t contained within the older store, meaning the load/store unit is able to combine data from both an in-flight store and data fetched from the L1 data cache. A dependent store+load pair has a latency of 6 cycles on the integer side, or 8 cycles on the vector/FP side. While Oryon 3 can’t do zero-latency store forwarding the way AMD’s Zen 5 and Intel’s Lion Cove can, the ability to avoid the 14 or 19 cycle penalty those cores take in partial overlap cases is quite nice. Arm’s Cortex X925 has the weakest store forwarding capabilities of the bunch, with no zero-cycle capability and a 12-13 cycle partial overlap penalty.
For independent accesses, Oryon 3 prefers 16B alignment for stores. Stores that cross a 16B boundary take a slight penalty, though curiously there’s no penalty for crossing a 64B cacheline boundary. Perhaps Oryon 3 has a special optimization for speeding up line-crossing stores. The same characteristics apply on the vector side.
SVE introduces scatter and gather functionality to the load/store unit, forcing it to handle possibly non-contiguous accesses from a single instruction. Testing with LD1W gathers (32-bit elements) achieves a core-wide throughput of 1-2 elements per cycle. Gathers therefore have lower throughput not just compared to contiguous loads, but also equivalent scalar loads. However, Oryon 3 has an optimization that allows repeated gather loads to the same address to execute at 4/cycle. Gathers therefore seem capable of using all four LSU pipes, and don’t go down a smaller subset of specialized pipes. However, the general case seems to rely on a complex flow that involves several micro-ops, resulting in lower throughput.
Dependent gathers have 14 cycle latency, which is acceptable for a non-contiguous load operation. Zen 5 handles vaguely equivalent AVX2 gathers with 19 cycle latency.
The load/store unit also has to translate program-visible virtual addresses to physical addresses that correspond to DRAM locations (or possibly MMIO). Qualcomm sized up the L1 DTLB from a 224 entry 7-way structure on Oryon 1, to a 256 entry 8-way one on Oryon 3. Perhaps Qualcomm always intended for the L1 DTLB to be 256 entries and 8-way set associative like the instruction-side L1 TLB, but couldn’t fit the last way into Oryon 1. A 256 entry L1 DTLB covers 1 MB of address space using 4 KB pages, which is a lot compared to the smaller L1 DTLBs on other designs. An 8K entry L2 TLB handles larger memory footprints, and serves both instruction and data accesses. The L2 TLB’s capacity is also impressive compared to the competition.
Comparing with Zen 5 can be complicated because AMD can opportunistically use a single TLB entry to cover up to four consecutive 4 KB pages, provided the translations have the same attributes and lead to contiguous physical pages. Zen 5 can cover more address space with its TLBs despite a lower entry count if it can make maximum use of that page coalescing capability, though I don’t have data on how effective that is in practice.
Testing with performance counters validates Qualcomm’s large TLB sizes. The core’s PMU indicates a rise in L1D TLB misses after 1 MB, when testing accesses with a 4 KB stride. L2 TLB misses rise after 32 MB, though they only sharply increase after 64 MB.
Qualcomm specifies 2-cycle latency for L2 TLB accesses, which would be incredible for a 8K entry L2 TLB. However, comparing L2 latency with 4 KB and 2 MB pages suggests that a L2 TLB hit costs at least an extra 6-7 cycles of latency.
Cache and Memory Access
Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X Elite used a two-level caching strategy that emphasizes speed over the ability to scale last level cache capacity and the number of cores served by each last level cache instance. For the Snapdragon X2 Elite Qualcomm upgraded the cache subsystem by increasing L2 capacity from 12 to 16 MB for the P-Core clusters. This cache capacity increase boosts the amount of cache a single core can allocate into. It also helps account for each cluster having six cores instead of four, though cache per core still drops slightly from 3 MB on Oryon 1 to 2.66 MB in Oryon 3.
16 MB of CPU-side last level cache isn’t large by 2026 standards. AMD’s standard Zen 5 configurations use 32 MB of L3 cache, while Intel’s Arrow Lake has 36 MB of L3. However, Qualcomm’s caching capacity is fine next to the 16 MB of L3 that AMD puts in their mainstream Strix Point mobile chip’s performance cluster, and Qualcomm makes their L2 fast for the capacity it provides. With 20-23 cycle latency depending on which core is making the access, Qualcomm’s L2 can return data faster than the 46 cycle latency that AMD’s optimization guide specifies for Zen 5’s L3. AMD’s 46 cycle figure seems to apply to configurations with 32 MB of L3, like on the Ryzen 9 9900X. A Zen 5 variant with 96 MB of L3 incurs several extra cycles of latency, showing how a triple level cache subsystem can enable last level cache capacity scaling because the core-private L2 cache reduces sensitivity to L3 latency. Intel’s Lion Cove is Oryon 3’s opposite with respect to caching strategy, with four cache levels to enable capacity/speed tradeoffs at L2 and L3.
20+ cycles of L2 latency is still high compared to 14 cycles on AMD’s Zen 5, so Oryon 3 uses a large 96 KB 6-way L1D. Unusually for a high frequency design, Oryon 3 achieves 3 cycle L1D latency. It’s an impressive achievement, because even Arm’s lower clocked Cortex X925 has 4 cycle latency to a smaller 64 KB L1D.

This type of prefetcher can follow pointer chasing chains and defeat latency testing if the tested chain falls within what the prefetcher can remember. Bandwidth
Oryon 3’s L1D can service four accesses per cycle, all four of which can be loads, and two of which can be stores. Compared to Zen 5 and Lion Cove, Oryon 3’s maximum load bandwidth is held back by its 128-bit vector width. However, Oryon 3 should remain very competitive when running code that can’t be well vectorized, or vectorized code that doesn’t scale to longer vector lengths.

However, AVX-512 does not give AMD a huge lead in SPEC’s floating point workloads. 749.fotonik3d and 765.roms execute a lot of AVX-512 instructions on Zen 5, but Oryon 3 is able to compensate with higher IPC. Third generation Oryon is a top-notch core with everything needed to succeed on a level playing field. Oryon 3 isn’t perfect of course. A wider SVE vector width could improve its situation relative to Zen 5 in vectorized workloads. Linux applications are also more likely to have aarch64 versions, minimising the importance of binary translation. articles.title: Qualcomm's Oryon 3 Reaches the Top
articles.body:
Qualcomm’s laptop effort had humble beginnings. Their early Arm-based laptops used cell phone SoCs, and suffered from noticeably poor performance even against lower end Intel chips. But breaking into the PC market was going to be a marathon rather than a sprint, and Qualcomm has been persistent. Qualcomm created higher performance Snapdragon variants targeted at laptops, which became increasingly competent with each generation. Now, Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme can deliver CPU performance that challenges the best of its x86-64 competition. To deliver that performance, Qualcomm relies on the third generation of their in-house Oryon architecture, which I’ll call Oryon 3 for short.
The Snapdragon X2 Elite deploys Oryon 3 in both E-Core and P-Core variants, which Qualcomm confusingly calls “performance” and “prime” cores, respectively. P-Cores are the star of the show in the Snapdragon X2 Elite, where they provide both maximum single threaded performance while also providing the bulk of multithreaded throughput. That’s because Qualcomm has P-Cores outnumber their E-Cores by a factor of two, creating an inverted hybrid strategy compared to Intel’s. Thanks to this strategy, Qualcomm’s Oryon 3 P-Core variant shoulders most of the burden when it comes to Qualcomm’s PC market ambitions.
Oryon 3 takes on this burden by deploying an architecture with a strong resemblance to the first Oryon generation. Qualcomm technically has a second generation Oryon core, but only used it in phones. Their website also suggests it’s a very minor change over the first generation, so I’ll be treating first generation Oryon as Oryon 3’s direct predecessor.
Similarity to Oryon 1 is a good thing, because that gives Oryon 3 just about everything you could ask for from a 2026-era high performance design. From Oryon 1, Oryon 3 inherits an out-of-order window in excess of 600 micro-ops. Qualcomm has also carried forward a two-level cache setup that emphasizes speed over capacity. Compared to its predecessor, Oryon 3 takes things up a notch by pushing clock speeds to 5 GHz. It’s a huge 16% increase over the 4.3 GHz speed that Oryon 1 could reach, and is enough to offer a generational performance gain on its own. But Qualcomm doesn’t stop there. Oryon 3 increases core width to 9 micro-ops, up from 8 in its predecessor, and makes a number of improvements throughout the pipeline. Qualcomm brings SVE2 and SME support to the new core as well, keeping it up-to-date with the evolving aarch64 architecture and opening up new software optimization opportunities. In its role as a maximum performance architecture, Oryon 3 faces off against the likes of AMD’s Zen 5 and Intel’s Lion Cove. Arm’s Cortex X925 is another competitor, thanks to Nvidia’s laptop push with N1X.
A Faster Frontend
Setting aside clock speed, Oryon 3’s headline architectural improvement is a core width increase from 8 to 9 ups. At the frontend, Qualcomm supports this by adding another decode slot. The fetch and decode pipeline otherwise looks mostly unchanged. Oryon 1 already had over-provisioned instruction cache bandwidth at 64 bytes per cycle, which is more than sufficient to feed a 8-wide or 9-wide aarch64 decoder. Qualcomm has also kept a 192 KB, 6-way instruction cache with hardware coherency, as well as a 256 entry 8-way instruction TLB. These large structures should help the core use its fastest instruction delivery path more often than its peers, which have smaller instruction caches and instruction TLBs. Impressively, Qualcomm managed to keep these large structures and add an extra decode slot while keeping a 13 cycle branch mispredict penalty. Clock speed increases often come with compromises like longer pipelines or smaller structures, but here Qualcomm is able to have their cake and eat it too.
Testing instruction bandwidth with a stream of NOPs validates the increased decoder width when the test loop fits within the instruction cache. Improvements continue at larger instruction footprints. Oryon 3 is able to sustain about 4 NOPs/cycle from L2, compared to 2 per cycle on Oryon 1. Qualcomm might have changed something with instruction prefetching from L2, or they might have widened datapaths between the instruction cache and L2. Whatever the case, Oryon 3 now matches the likes of AMD’s Zen 5 and Intel’s Lion Coves in terms of streaming code from L2, while boasting a much larger L2. AMD and Intel’s cores do have a L3 that provides more capacity than Qualcomm’s L2, but fetching code from that L3 will cause another drop in instruction throughput.
High core throughput places pressure on the branch predictor, which must follow the instruction stream fast enough to keep the core fed. Oryon 3 improves by expanding its predecessor’s ability to handle taken branches back-to-back. Oryon 1 could only do “zero-bubble” taken branches within a 8 KB instruction footprint. Oryon 3 can do so within a 2048 branch footprint, regardless of branch spacing and code footprint. Perhaps Qualcomm switched to using a fully decoupled 2048 entry BTB. Realistically, that means Oryon 3 should be able to do zero-bubble taken branches over a branch footprint 2x to 4x larger than its predecessor, considering typical branch spacing.
Compared to AMD and Intel’s latest cores, Qualcomm lacks any ability to handle more than one taken branch per cycle. Arm’s newer cores are also capable of doing two taken branches per cycle. I suspect AMD, Arm, and Intel decided that handling multiple taken branches per cycle became more profitable once their cores got wide enough, so seeing Qualcomm build a very wide core without that ability is surprising. Perhaps clock speed factors into that decision, because going from 4.3 to 5 GHz is a huge jump. If so, Qualcomm’s choice would be justified because a clock speed increase of that magnitude probably offers a larger performance increase than going for two taken branches per cycle. Of course, it’s impossible to know if branch predictor paths presented a timing challenge for Oryon.
For branches with dynamic taken/not-taken behavior, Oryon 3 has a 2-cycle conditional predictor. Testing with branches whose outcomes correlate with increasingly long history lengths shows an average 0.5 cycle increase in time per branch over an always- taken reference run, as long as the test stays within the conditional predictor’s capabilities. Because I randomly generate patterns so that each branch is taken roughly 50% of the time, a 0.5 cycle average penalty suggests Qualcomm only incurs the 2-cycle timing if the direction predictor disagrees with a base prediction. Direction prediction starts falling apart with more than 32K patterns in play, which is an improvement over the approximately 24K patterns that first generation Oryon could handle in this test.
For comparison, Zen 5’s conditional predictor can handle roughly 48K patterns before falling apart. Unlike Oryon 3, and unlike some older Zen generations, Zen 5 does not show an increase in branch latency compared to an always-taken pattern.
Indirect branches can go to multiple targets, and present another level of difficulty because the branch predictor has to select between previously seen targets, and must store more than one target per branch. Oryon 3 has a 2-cycle indirect predictor that can track 2048 indirect targets, matching its predecessor.
A single branch can jump to 256 targets without incurring a significant penalty. This could mean at least eight of the bits that Oryon 3 uses to index into its indirect target array are influenced by branch history.
A 50 entry return stack handles return predictions, just as on Oryon 1. However, testing shows that Oryon 3 can use all 50 entries before hitting a performance degradation. When call depth exceeds return stack capacity, Oryon 3 degrades gracefully rather than immediately taking a drastic penalty as Oryon 1 does. Oryon 1’s performance drop is heavy enough to suggest it’s mispredicting every return after the return stack overflows.
Perhaps Qualcomm implemented a new mechanism to keep a single overflow from messing up the entire return stack, and lets Oryon 3 only mispredict returns whose addresses get forced out on an overflow. Whatever this optimization is, it gives Oryon 3 return prediction behavior in-line with many other cores, including AMD’s Zen 5 and Intel’s Skymont. In capacity terms, AMD’s Zen 5 has a slightly larger 52 entry return stack.
Rename/Allocate Optimizations
Optimizations at the rename and allocate stage on Qualcomm’s big core are remarkably similar to those on its little core counterpart. Both cores can eliminate up to two register-to-register MOVs per cycle. They can also eliminate up to two add-immediate instructions, as long as their immediates sum to 255 or less. It’s slightly strange that Qualcomm has kept the same optimization capability even though the big core is more than twice as wide as its little core companion. That results in degraded microbenchmark figures when I chain dependent MOVs or add-immediate instructions without a break, because the wider core can get more of those instructions into the same rename group, which means the two-per-cycle restriction causes more missed optimization opportunities.

One of the best strategies in CPU architecture is to avoid changing something that isn’t broken. Oryon 3’s backend at a high level is basically identical to the one in its predecessor. Register files and memory ordering queues see little to no movement in size as well.
Qualcomm’s choice to avoid major backend changes is justified, because Oryon 3’s backend structures remain competitively sized even against emerging competition like AMD’s Zen 6. Execution throughput also remains competitive. Oryon 3 does have slightly smaller memory ordering queues, and weaker vector execution throughput compared to its x86-64 counterparts. The latter comes down to having a smaller 128-bit vector width, which is especially a disadvantage against Zen 5. However, that should only affect a small minority of applications.

The predicate registers themselves only have to be 16 bits wide because of Oryon 3’s 128-bit vector length. But while the predicate register file doesn’t need a lot of storage, it does need to be hooked up to every major execution unit block. Predicate generation can happen from both the scalar and vector side. All four vector pipes and four load/store pipes support predication, meaning a lot of reads from the predicate register file.
New SVE2 and SME instructions also require changes to backend logic. SVE’s vector length agnostic design rides heavily on predicate generation instructions like those of the WHILE* variety (like WHILELO). Oryon 3 breaks WHILE* instructions into two micro-ops, which execute through the integer pipes to deliver a throughput of one WHILE* instruction per cycle. Predicate generation instructions that don’t require a GPR input, like PTRUE and CMPEQ, execute through two FP/vector pipes. Besides predication focused changes, SVE2 adds new math instructions like CDOT, meaning more execution unit functionality behind the vector/FP ports.
Load/Store
Like Oryon 1, Oryon 3 has a four-pipe load/store unit. Memory dependencies are handled by a robust store forwarding mechanism, which can do fast forwarding for all cases where a load overlaps a prior store. Oryon 3 is able to do that even when the load isn’t contained within the older store, meaning the load/store unit is able to combine data from both an in-flight store and data fetched from the L1 data cache. A dependent store+load pair has a latency of 6 cycles on the integer side, or 8 cycles on the vector/FP side. While Oryon 3 can’t do zero-latency store forwarding the way AMD’s Zen 5 and Intel’s Lion Cove can, the ability to avoid the 14 or 19 cycle penalty those cores take in partial overlap cases is quite nice. Arm’s Cortex X925 has the weakest store forwarding capabilities of the bunch, with no zero-cycle capability and a 12-13 cycle partial overlap penalty.
For independent accesses, Oryon 3 prefers 16B alignment for stores. Stores that cross a 16B boundary take a slight penalty, though curiously there’s no penalty for crossing a 64B cacheline boundary. Perhaps Oryon 3 has a special optimization for speeding up line-crossing stores. The same characteristics apply on the vector side.
SVE introduces scatter and gather functionality to the load/store unit, forcing it to handle possibly non-contiguous accesses from a single instruction. Testing with LD1W gathers (32-bit elements) achieves a core-wide throughput of 1-2 elements per cycle. Gathers therefore have lower throughput not just compared to contiguous loads, but also equivalent scalar loads. However, Oryon 3 has an optimization that allows repeated gather loads to the same address to execute at 4/cycle. Gathers therefore seem capable of using all four LSU pipes, and don’t go down a smaller subset of specialized pipes. However, the general case seems to rely on a complex flow that involves several micro-ops, resulting in lower throughput.
Dependent gathers have 14 cycle latency, which is acceptable for a non-contiguous load operation. Zen 5 handles vaguely equivalent AVX2 gathers with 19 cycle latency.
The load/store unit also has to translate program-visible virtual addresses to physical addresses that correspond to DRAM locations (or possibly MMIO). Qualcomm sized up the L1 DTLB from a 224 entry 7-way structure on Oryon 1, to a 256 entry 8-way one on Oryon 3. A 256 entry L1 DTLB covers 1 MB of address space using 4 KB pages, which is a lot compared to the smaller L1 DTLBs on other designs. Comparing with Zen 5 can be complicated because AMD can opportunistically use a single TLB entry to cover up to four consecutive 4 KB pages, provided the translations have the same attributes and lead to contiguous physical pages. Zen 5 can cover more address space with its TLBs despite a lower entry count if it can make maximum use of that page coalescing capability, though I don’t have data on how effective that is in practice.
Testing with performance counters validates Qualcomm’s large TLB sizes. The core’s PMU indicates a rise in L1D TLB misses after 1 MB, when testing accesses with a 4 KB stride. L2 TLB misses rise after 32 MB, though they only sharply increase after 64 MB.
Qualcomm specifies 2-cycle latency for L2 TLB accesses, which would be incredible for a 8K entry L2 TLB. However, comparing L2 latency with 4 KB and 2 MB pages suggests that a L2 TLB hit costs at least an extra 6-7 cycles of latency.

The laptop is subjectively as fast as my desktop back at home, and shows just how far Qualcomm has gone. I want to see the people who worked on it rewarded for what they achieved. I also hope to see the Oryon line grow with future generations, and keep pushing the leading edge of single threaded performance.
