articles.title: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies aged 65
articles.body:
Tributes for Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor after his death aged 65
- Published
Simon Le Bon, Sir Rod Stewart and Gary Kemp are among the pop stars who have paid tribute to Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor following his death at the age of 65.
Taylor co-wrote some of the group's biggest hits including Save A Prayer, Rio and Girls On Film.
Le Bon and his bandmates paid tribute, saying "he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music", while Sir Rod remembered his "dear pal" and Spandau Ballet's Kemp called him "a great player who set the tone for the 80s".
Taylor's wife Tracey called him "the rock of our family", adding: "We will miss him every single day." He died after "a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer", Duran Duran said in a statement on Wednesday.
- Andy Taylor: Duran Duran's livewire guitarist who was a Wild Boy on stage and off 
  - Published19 hours ago
He died "peacefully at home, surrounded by his family, on Monday 23rd November", a statement said.
Paying tribute, his Duran Duran bandmates said: "From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music.
"His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed."
They said their thoughts were with his wife, children and grandson.
Le Bon said there was a "a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart".
"Andy never took the easy musical route. His overdrive overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the New Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later."
Sir Rod, who wrote five songs with Taylor for the 1988 album Out of Order, recalled them making "some good music together" and having "some outrageous fun".
Kemp said Taylor "influenced many of us along the way with his sparse staccato style", adding: "He brought shameless rock to the mix."
In a band tribute, Spandau Ballet called him "a hugely talented musician and an important part of the British music scene".
US guitarist Nile Rodgers, the co-founder of Chic, recalled "countless great days and nights" with his "dear friend".
Belinda Carlisle said she was "blessed" to have worked with Taylor, who played the guitar solo and was in the video for her song Mad About You.
Former Led Zeppelin frontman Robert Plant called Taylor "a tough fighter", while Then Jerico's Mark Shaw remembered him as "one of the greatest musicians and songwriters I've ever heard and had the privilege to work with".
Taylor's wife Tracey, a hairstylist he met during the early days of Duran Duran, and whom he married in 1982, said: "For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first for Taylor, adding: "Nothing made him happier than having us all together."
She said he faced the last few years "with so much courage and determination" and said they were "grateful" for the "kindness and support shown to him by fans throughout his illness", saying it brought him "immense comfort and strength".
The son of a fisherman, Taylor taught himself guitar, bass, and drums and began playing professionally at age 13.
He played with several bands around the UK before answering a music paper advertisement for a "live-wire guitarist", which led to his audition for Duran Duran in Birmingham in April 1980.
The group went on to achieve global fame through the New Romantic movement, which combined slick, melodic synth-pop with aspirational music videos and chiselled good looks.
Taylor's guitar lines - full of glassy, powerful riffs - were often a highlight of their songs, from the choppy opening of Girls on Film to the sleazy scuzz of Hungry Like The Wolf.
Duran Duran were one of the biggest pop acts of the 1980s, and its five members became global hearththrobs.
Their indelible hooks and airbrushed music videos found a natural home on the newly launched MTV, giving their career a huge boost in the US.
They became so popular in the US that the press labeled them the leaders of a "second British invasion" of the charts - alongside groups like Spandau Ballet, Human League and Eurythmics.
During a hiatus in 1984, Andy and John Taylor enlisted Robert Palmer for their successful but short-lived side project the Power Station.
The following year, the guitarist decided to quit Duran Duran after a miserable experience performing at Live Aid.
"We'd reached rock bottom and we had absolutely nothing to say to each other," he wrote in his autobiography, Wild Boy.
"We drove to the venue through streets packed with excited rock fans, but inside the bus the atmosphere was as if we were on a way to a funeral."
He went on to play on Palmer's Addicted To Love, and released a solo album, Thunder, in 1987.
After a period writing and producing albums for other artists, he rejoined Duran Duran in 2000, lasting for just one album (2004's Astronaut) before parting ways again.
In 2022, when the band were inducted to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, Taylor was notably absent from the ceremony, despite public plans for a reunion.
When the group took the stage, Le Bon read a letter from the guitarist, in which he revealed his diagnosis with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer.
Nonetheless, he contributed to the following year's Halloween-themed album Danse Macabre, marking his final collaboration with the band.
The following BBC programmes will pay tribute to Taylor:
- Duran Duran at the BBC, on BBC Four on Friday 27 November at 21:30 GMT
- Sounds of the 80s, on Radio 2 on Saturday 28 November at at 18:00 GMT

articles.title: Defang Security Incident
articles.body:
On November 12, 2026 an attacker copied the credentials we use to run Defang and downloaded a copy of our main database. Here is what happened, what was exposed, what we have done, and what you should do.
On November 12, 2026 an attacker got into the Defang Deploy build system and copied the credentials we use to run Defang. With those they downloaded a copy of our main database. We confirmed this on November 23, 2026. If you have a Defang Portal account, your account is in that database, and this post explains what was taken and what you should do. We are also writing to every affected user by email.
If you installed the Defang GitHub App, some of those credentials could also be used against your GitHub repositories and your cloud account. We have replaced them, but there are checks only you can do. They are listed under "What you should do" below. Please go through them as soon as you can.
What happened
We used a separate GitHub App for local development and testing. It was installed on two of our own repositories and had more permissions than it needed, including permission to change deployment environments. Acting as that app, the attacker pushed a commit to one of those repositories and tagged it as a release. Our production environment trusted release tags, so their code ran in our CI with access to our production credentials, and the attacker copied them.
The activity we can see ran from about 06:00 to 10:30 UTC on November 12. The credentials stayed valid until we replaced them on November 23. We are still checking whether they were used after November 12. Some of our logs are not detailed enough to rule that out, so we will update this post when we know more.
Timeline
All times are UTC.
- November 12, 06:05: the first workflow that copied build credentials ran, against our development and staging environments.
- November 12, 06:26: our production credentials were copied.
- November 12, 07:57 to 08:10: the database was copied.
- November 15: we were made aware of a security issue with a dependency and installed the update.
- November 23: a routine security scan found suspicious activity in our repositories.
- November 23: we confirmed the database copy from our access logs, replaced our production credentials and emailed every affected user.
- November 24: we published this post.
What the attacker could see
- Your name and email address. This is the address only: the attacker did not get into your email account or see any of your messages.
- Your GitHub or GitLab username, and the names of the organizations that account belongs to
- The answers you gave when you signed up
- If you installed the Defang GitHub App: the names of the repositories it can access, including private ones
- The cloud accounts you connected to Defang (account, project or subscription IDs and regions; no credentials)
- The Compose files you deployed or generated with Defang
- Copies of deployment state from deploys between October 12 and November 19. These can include database passwords and any environment variable built from a defang config value, such as a database URL that contains a password.
If you installed the Defang GitHub App: what the attacker could use
The attacker could use the Defang GitHub App's key, and the GitHub sign-in token we keep when you connect GitHub. The token was stored encrypted, but the encryption key was taken too. Until we replaced them on November 23, anyone holding these could do in your repositories what the app is allowed to do:
- push commits and branches
- change workflow files and start workflow runs
- overwrite Actions secrets and variables
- change deployment environments and their protection rules
- open and merge pull requests
- change repository settings, including branch protection, deploy keys and collaborators
A workflow run started this way can receive your cloud credentials, because the role Defang set up for GitHub deploys trusts workflows in your repository.
If you have billing details with us
The copied credentials included a key for our account at Stripe, our payment provider. Until we replaced it on November 23, someone holding that key could read the record Stripe keeps for you:
- your name and email address
- your billing address, or the parts of it you gave us, and your tax ID if you entered one
- the brand, last four digits and expiry date of your card
- your subscription and invoice history
Your full card number and security code were not exposed. Stripe holds those and does not make them available to Defang or to anyone using our key.
What was not exposed
- Passwords. Defang has none for you: you sign in with GitHub, GitLab or an emailed code.
- Your cloud credentials. We never hold them. Your BYOC deployments run in your own account with your own credentials, and Defang's servers have no direct access to that account or to anything running in it. The one indirect path is the GitHub Actions deploy role described above.
- The contents of your repositories. They are not stored in our database.
- Config values you set with defang config. They stay in your cloud account, except for the copies in deployment state described above.
What we have done
- Replaced the Defang GitHub App key and secrets on November 23, and revoked the GitHub sign-in tokens we held.
- Replaced our other production credentials, including database, payment and email credentials, on November 23.
- Signed out every session and invalidated every Defang access token issued before November 23.
- Stopped keeping copies of deployment state on November 19 and deleted the copies we had.
- Cancelled every pending cloud invite link. If you were inviting someone, send a new invite.
- Notified GitHub, who are helping us audit for token misuse.
- Installed the security update on November 15.
- Revoked the development GitHub App's credentials and suspended the app on November 23.
- Reverted the production and staging deployment configurations that were altered by the attacker.
- Notified users and relevant authorities of the data breach.
What you should do
Everyone
- Be careful with email that claims to come from Defang, GitHub or GitLab, especially anything that asks you to sign in, approve an app or share a code. Someone holding this data can write a convincing message that uses your real name and username. We will never ask you for a password or a token by email.
- You will need to sign in to Defang again.
If you installed the Defang GitHub App: in GitHub
- Check your connected repositories for activity you don't recognize since November 11:
  - new commits, branches or tags
  - changes under .github/workflows
  - workflow runs you didn't start
  - changed Actions secrets or variables
  - new deploy keys or collaborators, and changed branch protection rules
- Look in particular at anything from defang-app[bot]. Your security log is at github.com/settings/security-log; organizations have an audit log under Settings.
- Lock down the deployment environments Defang created. In each connected repository, open Settings, then Environments. For every environment whose name starts with defang-, set "Deployment branches and tags" to your deploy branch only. You can also add required reviewers. This stops a workflow on any other branch from receiving your cloud credentials.
- Revoke and reconnect Defang's access to your GitHub account. In GitHub, go to Settings, then Applications, then Authorized GitHub Apps, and revoke Defang. Sign in to Defang again afterwards.
- If you no longer deploy from GitHub with Defang, uninstall the Defang app from your account or organization.
If you deploy from GitHub Actions: in your cloud account
- Check who has used your deploy role since November 11. The role or identity Defang set up for GitHub deploys has administrator access to your account. A token from a branch or workflow you don't deploy from is a sign of misuse.
  - On AWS this is usually defang-cd-CIRole. Search CloudTrail for AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity calls on it.
  - On Google Cloud, check the workload identity pool's token exchanges.
  - On Azure, check the sign-in logs for the managed identity.
- Narrow that role's trust to the branch or environment you deploy from, if it currently allows any branch.
If you deployed with Defang between October 12 and November 19
- Change your database passwords and any secret that was part of another environment variable, then redeploy. Use defang config set <NAME> for each one.
- If your Compose file has secrets written directly in it, change those too.
If you have billing details with us
You do not need to replace your card. The exposed details are not enough to charge it. Watch your statements as you normally would, and be wary of email or calls that quote your last four digits or billing address to appear legitimate.
If any of these checks turns up something you don't recognize
Rotate the secrets in that repository's Actions secrets and environments and the cloud credentials its workflows can reach, then tell us.
Frequently asked questions
Was my GitHub password exposed? Do I need to change it right away?
No. Defang never had your GitHub password. You sign in with GitHub, GitLab or an emailed code, so there is no password for us to lose.
What the attacker could use was the Defang GitHub App's key and the GitHub sign-in token we keep when you connect GitHub. We replaced the key and revoked those tokens on November 23. Changing your GitHub password is not required, but it does no harm, and turning on two-factor authentication is a good idea in any case. The checks that matter are the ones under "If you installed the Defang GitHub App: in GitHub" above: look for activity you don't recognize, lock down deployment environments, and revoke the Defang GitHub App.
Did they take only my information from GitHub, or did they go further? Did they get my email?
They got your email address, but not your email account. The address we have on file for you is in our database, so it was copied. Defang has no access to your mailbox, so the attacker could not read your email or sign in to your email account through us.
From GitHub, what we hold is your username, the names of the organizations your account belongs to and, if you installed the Defang GitHub App, the names of the repositories it can access. The contents of your repositories are not in our database.
If you installed the Defang GitHub App, the attacker also held the credentials that let them act in your repositories until we replaced them on November 23. We are still checking whether they were used after November 12, and we will update this post when we know more. That is why we ask you to review your repositories and your cloud account. "What the attacker could see" and "What the attacker could use" above list everything.
Did this happen only to me, or to all users?
Anyone with a Defang Portal account is in the database that was copied, so your email address, and potentially your name, was exposed along with everyone else's. Beyond that, what was exposed depends on how you use Defang. See above section for details.
How can I protect my data? How do I check that an email really comes from you?
- Don't sign in, approve an app or share a code because an email asked you to. Open the Defang Portal, GitHub or GitLab yourself by typing the address in your browser, rather than following a link in a message.
- We will never ask you for a password or a token by email.
- Someone holding this data can quote your real name, username or the organizations you belong to. A message that knows those details is not proof that it comes from us.

articles.title: Defang Security Incident
articles.body:
On November 12, 2026 an attacker copied the credentials we use to run Defang and downloaded a copy of our main database. Here is what happened, what was exposed, what we have done, and what you should do.
On November 12, 2026 an attacker got into the Defang Deploy build system and copied the credentials we use to run Defang. With those they downloaded a copy of our main database. We confirmed this on November 23, 2026. If you have a Defang Portal account, your account is in that database, and this post explains what was taken and what you should do. We are also writing to every affected user by email.
If you installed the Defang GitHub App, some of those credentials could also be used against your GitHub repositories and your cloud account. We have replaced them, but there are checks only you can do. They are listed under "What you should do" below. Please go through them as soon as you can.
What happened
We used a separate GitHub App for local development and testing. It was installed on two of our own repositories and had more permissions than it needed, including permission to change deployment environments. Acting as that app, the attacker pushed a commit to one of those repositories and tagged it as a release. Our production environment trusted release tags, so their code ran in our CI with access to our production credentials, and the attacker copied them.
The activity we can see ran from about 06:00 to 10:30 UTC on November 12. The credentials stayed valid until we replaced them on November 23. We are still checking whether they were used after November 12. Some of our logs are not detailed enough to rule that out, so we will update this post when we know more.
Timeline
All times are UTC.
- November 12, 06:05: the first workflow that copied build credentials ran, against our development and staging environments.
- November 12, 06:26: our production credentials were copied.
- November 12, 07:57 to 08:10: the database was copied.
- November 15: we were made aware of a security issue with a dependency and installed the update.
- November 23: a routine security scan found suspicious activity in our repositories.
- November 23: we confirmed the database copy from our access logs, replaced our production credentials and emailed every affected user.
- November 24: we published this post.
What the attacker could see
- Your name and email address. This is the address only: the attacker did not get into your email account or see any of your messages.
- Your GitHub or GitLab username, and the names of the organizations that account belongs to
- The answers you gave when you signed up
- If you installed the Defang GitHub App: the names of the repositories it can access, including private ones
- The cloud accounts you connected to Defang (account, project or subscription IDs and regions; no credentials)
- The Compose files you deployed or generated with Defang
- Copies of deployment state from deploys between October 12 and November 19. These can include database passwords and any environment variable built from a defang config value, such as a database URL that contains a password.
If you installed the Defang GitHub App: what the attacker could use
The attacker could use the Defang GitHub App's key, and the GitHub sign-in token we keep when you connect GitHub. The token was stored encrypted, but the encryption key was taken too. Until we replaced them on November 23, anyone holding these could do in your repositories what the app is allowed to do:
- push commits and branches
- change workflow files and start workflow runs
- overwrite Actions secrets and variables
- change deployment environments and their protection rules
- open and merge pull requests
- change repository settings, including branch protection, deploy keys and collaborators
A workflow run started this way can receive your cloud credentials, because the role Defang set up for GitHub deploys trusts workflows in your repository.
If you have billing details with us
The copied credentials included a key for our account at Stripe, our payment provider. Until we replaced it on November 23, someone holding that key could read the record Stripe keeps for you:
- your name and email address
- your billing address, or the parts of it you gave us, and your tax ID if you entered one
- the brand, last four digits and expiry date of your card
- your subscription and invoice history
Your full card number and security code were not exposed. Stripe holds those and does not make them available to Defang or to anyone using our key.
What was not exposed
- Passwords. Defang has none for you: you sign in with GitHub, GitLab or an emailed code.
- Your cloud credentials. We never hold them. Your BYOC deployments run in your own account with your own credentials, and Defang's servers have no direct access to that account or to anything running in it. The one indirect path is the GitHub Actions deploy role described above.
- The contents of your repositories. They are not stored in our database.
- Config values you set with defang config. They stay in your cloud account, except for the copies in deployment state described above.
What we have done
- Replaced the Defang GitHub App key and secrets on November 23, and revoked the GitHub sign-in tokens we held.
- Replaced our other production credentials, including database, payment and email credentials, on November 23.
- Signed out every session and invalidated every Defang access token issued before November 23.
- Stopped keeping copies of deployment state on November 19 and deleted the copies we had.
- Cancelled every pending cloud invite link. If you were inviting someone, send a new invite.
- Notified GitHub, who are helping us audit for token misuse.
- Installed the security update on November 15.
- Revoked the development GitHub App's credentials and suspended the app on November 23.
- Reverted the production and staging deployment configurations that were altered by the attacker.
- Notified users and relevant authorities of the data breach.
What you should do
Everyone
- Be careful with email that claims to come from Defang, GitHub or GitLab, especially anything that asks you to sign in, approve an app or share a code. Someone holding this data can write a convincing message that uses your real name and username. We will never ask you for a password or a token by email.
- You will need to sign in to Defang again.
If you installed the Defang GitHub App: in GitHub
- Check your connected repositories for activity you don't recognize since November 11:
  - new commits, branches or tags
  - changes under .github/workflows
  - workflow runs you didn't start
  - changed Actions secrets or variables
  - new deploy keys or collaborators, and changed branch protection rules
- Look in particular at anything from defang-app[bot]. Your security log is at github.com/settings/security-log; organizations have an audit log under Settings.
- Lock down the deployment environments Defang created. In each connected repository, open Settings, then Environments. For every environment whose name starts with defang-, set "Deployment branches and tags" to your deploy branch only. You can also add required reviewers. This stops a workflow on any other branch from receiving your cloud credentials.
- Revoke and reconnect Defang's access to your GitHub account. In GitHub, go to Settings, then Applications, then Authorized GitHub Apps, and revoke Defang. Sign in to Defang again afterwards.
- If you no longer deploy from GitHub with Defang, uninstall the Defang app from your account or organization.

- Check who has used your deploy role since November 11. The role or identity Defang set up for GitHub deploys has administrator access to your account. A token from a branch or workflow you don't deploy from is a sign of misuse.
  - On AWS this is usually defang-cd-CIRole. Search CloudTrail for AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity calls on it.
  - On Google Cloud, check the workload identity pool's token exchanges.
  - On Azure, check the sign-in logs for the managed identity.
- Narrow that role's trust to the branch or environment you deploy from, if it currently allows any branch.

- Change your database passwords and any secret that was part of another environment variable, then redeploy. Use defang config set <NAME> for each one.
- If your Compose file has secrets written directly in it, change those too.

You do not need to replace your card. The exposed details are not enough to charge it. Watch your statements as you normally would, and be wary of email or calls that quote your last four digits or billing address to appear legitimate.
If any of these checks turns up something you don't recognize
Rotate the secrets in that repository's Actions secrets and environments and the cloud credentials its workflows can reach, then tell us.

No. Defang never had your GitHub password. You sign in with GitHub, GitLab or an emailed code, so there is no password for us to lose.
What the attacker could use was the Defang GitHub App's key and the GitHub sign-in token we keep when you connect GitHub. We replaced the key and revoked those tokens on November 23. Changing your GitHub password is not required, but it does no harm, and turning on two-factor authentication is a good idea in any case. The checks that matter are the ones under "If you installed the Defang GitHub App: in GitHub" above: look for activity you don't recognize, lock down deployment environments, and revoke the Defang GitHub App.

They got your email address, but not your email account. The address we have on file for you is in our database, so it was copied. Defang has no access to your mailbox, so the attacker could not read your email or sign in to your email account through us.
From GitHub, what we hold is your username, the names of the organizations your account belongs to and, if you installed the Defang GitHub App, the names of the repositories it can access. The contents of your repositories are not in our database.
If you installed the Defang GitHub App, the attacker also held the credentials that let them act in your repositories until we replaced them on November 23. We are still checking whether they were used after November 12, and we will update this post when we know more. That is why we ask you to review your repositories and your cloud account. "What the attacker could see" and "What the attacker could use" above list everything.
Did this happen only to me, or to all users?
Anyone with a Defang Portal account is in the database that was copied, so your email address, and potentially your name, was exposed along with everyone else's. Beyond that, what was exposed depends on how you use Defang. See above section for details.
How can I protect my data? How do I check that an email really comes from you?
- Don't sign in, approve an app or share a code because an email asked you to. Open the Defang Portal, GitHub or GitLab yourself by typing the address in your browser, rather than following a link in a message.
- We will never ask you for a password or a token by email.
- Someone holding this data can quote your real name, username or the organizations you belong to. A message that knows those details is not proof that it comes from us.
- If you are unsure about a message, forward it to sec@defang.io and we will tell you whether we sent it.
- Work through the checklist in "What you should do" above. In short: review your repositories, review your cloud account, change database passwords and secrets if you deployed between October 12 and November 19, and turn on two-factor authentication on your GitHub and cloud accounts.
How do I delete my account and data?
Open Settings in the Defang Portal and delete your account there, or email sec@defang.io and we will do it for you.
Contact us
If you find anything suspicious, or want an engineer to go through your account, repositories or cloud account with you, write to sec@defang.io. We will update this post as we learn more.

articles.title: Intel One Mono font
articles.body:
Introducing Intel One Mono, an expressive monospaced font family that’s built with clarity, legibility, and the needs of developers in mind.
It’s easier to read, and available for free, with an open-source font license.
Identifying the typographically underserved low-vision developer audience, Frere-Jones Type designed the Intel One Mono typeface in partnership with the Intel Brand Team and VMLY&R, for maximum legibility to address developers' fatigue and eyestrain and reduce coding errors. A panel of low-vision and legally blind developers provided feedback at each stage of design.
Intel One Mono also covers a wide range of over 200 languages using the Latin script. The Intel One Mono fonts are provided in four weights — Light, Regular, Medium, and Bold — with matching italics, and we are happy to share both an official release of fonts ready to use as well as editable sources.
To install the fonts, please use the provided builds under Releases. Please refer to your software’s documentation for how to activate and use these fonts.
- VSCode - In Settings, search Font Family, then specify Intel One Mono
- Sublime Text - Go to Sublime Text -> Preferences -> Settings and set font_face to Intel One Mono
- IntelliJ Platform - Go to File -> Settings -> Editor -> Font and set Font to Intel One Mono
- We recommend the .otf or .ttf format for desktop use.
- The .ttf files are also well suited for mobile apps.
- The .woff and .woff2 fonts are optimized for web use.
We recommend using these fonts at 7 points and larger in print, 9 pixels and larger on screen. The .ttf, .woff and .woff2 fonts provided in the official release have been manually optimized for screen display, improving clarity and legibility, especially on Windows platforms.
Outside of the default characters, there are a few extra features that are accessible in some applications, as well as via CSS:
- Programming Ligatures: To use programming ligatures, activate the ss01 feature (Stylistic Set #1). Additional refinements are available via ss02 and ss03: Stylistic Set #2 switches the <= and >= combinations to arrow forms (math contractions being the default otherwise), and Stylistic Set #3 additionally activates a “www” ligature.
- Alternate three: New in release 1.5. Alternate form for three added. The round top three, numerator, denomenator, superior and inferior can be activated with stylistic Set #4.
- Raised Colon: The colon is automatically raised in operators, to align with math symbols. For non-programming contexts, the raised colon can be applied contextually between numbers or activated generally. The contextual option is available via ss11 (Stylistic Set #11); for the global switch use ss12 (Stylistic Set #12) or salt (Stylistic Alternates).
- Language Support: ccmp and locl features ensure correct display across a wide range of languages. These are usually active by default. We recommend setting the language tag/setting in your software to the desired language for best results.
- Superior/superscript and inferior/subscript figures are included via their Unicode codepoints, or you can produce them from the default figures via the sups (Superscript) and subs/sinf (Subscript) features.
- Fraction numerals are similarly available via the numr (Numerator) and dnom (Denominator) features. A set of premade fractions is also available in the fonts.
Programming ligatures are not active by default. To use them, activate the stylistic sets of your preference in your code editor. For example:
- VSCode - In Settings, add "editor.fontLigatures": "'ss01'"
- Sublime Text - In Settings, add "font_options": ["ss01"]
You will find editable sources in the sources directory. The instances subfolder contains separate source files for each style of the typeface. Sources are provided in .ufo files, which contain complete artwork, links to OpenType features provided in separate .fea files, as well as meta information like naming and vertical alignments for each style of the typeface.
These are not installable fonts, but rather the source files that produce them: UFO (Unified Font Object) is an open, human-readable font source file format; you can find the file spec here. These sources were created using RoboFont. Many other font editors will also be able to open .ufo files; we recommend using RoboFont version 4.4.
For instances, you will find postscript and truetype subfolders; these contain separate source files for the .otf format and the .ttf/.woff/.woff2 files respectively. Since the format for the outline drawings differs between these sets of formats, for best results we recommend using the postscript sources to create .otf fonts, and the TrueType sources to create .ttf, .woff, or .woff2 fonts.
After making your desired edits, you can generate installable fonts directly from the font editor using its “Generate Font” functionality. If you use RoboFont, any install options should default to the ideal settings, but here they are for reference:
- For .otf builds, we recommend activating “Decompose” as well as “Autohint” options.
- For .ttf, .woff and .woff2 builds, we recommend activating the “Autohint” option only (see note on hinting below).
- In any case, we recommend using the “Release Mode” setting for best results.
If you would like to apply edits across multiple weights, a more advanced yet potentially efficient way is to edit the masters. These are special sources that describe the extreme points in the design space — the lightest and heaviest weights for both roman and italic designs.
After editing masters, you will need to rerun interpolation to generate individual weights and styles within that design space. This requires the .designspace files enclosed with the masters. The designspace format is an open, XML-based format that describes interpolation spaces (format specification for reference). For a RoboFont-based workflow we recommend Skateboard for interpolation; you can also use the free DesignSpaceEditor extension to view and edit these files.
Note that masters are only available in postscript format, so they will be best for creating .otf fonts. If you need to make TrueType based builds from the masters, we recommend QuadraticConverter for best quality conversion of the curves before generating .ttf, .woff, or .woff2 files; mind that the results will not match the provided instances precisely.
NB: The prepared instances contain some additional data that cannot be maintained through interpolation. For best results, compare new interpolations to the existing instance sources and update them accordingly, specifically the information accessible through the Font Info panels.
For TrueType-based formats (.ttf, .woff, .woff2 files), the official releases are manually optimized for screen rendering. These “hinting” sources are stored separately from the .ufo files, which do not contain any TrueType hinting information. When rebuilding TrueType-based formats, we recommend using the “autohint” option to achieve reasonable, though not identical screen rendering.
If you would like to access and edit manual hinting instructions, you will find these in the separate set of source files under hinting/truetype hinting source. These special TTF files will be viewable and editable using Microsoft VTT.
If you have requests for edits or additions to the official releases, please open issues and we will try to accomodate them.

articles.title: S&P considers Nvidia credit downgrade over governance and ‘key man’ risks
articles.body:
S&P Global Ratings, one of the three major credit rating agencies, is considering downgrading Nvidia’s rating, citing concerns about the company’s management and governance practices.
Despite Nvidia’s strong financial performance, the ouster and reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang has raised concerns about “weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning” and “key man risk,” meaning heavy reliance on Huang for its future success, S&P said in a statement.
The agency expects to finish its review within 90 days and could cut Nvidia’s rating from AA to AA-, the fourth-highest on its scale.
Although Nvidia is certain to keep its investment-grade rating, a downgrade could raise its borrowing costs. Because Nvidia backstops neoclouds and other infrastructure companies that lack strong credit on their own, a lower rating could make their debt costlier or force them to post more collateral.
In August, Nvidia announced plans to arrange $500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure with six financial institutions, including Goldman Sachs, Apollo, and Blackstone. Under the original terms, Nvidia would guarantee 25% of the loans. But even before Huang’s ouster and return, lenders had been demanding that Nvidia guarantee more, Bloomberg reported.
A downgrade would likely prompt lenders to demand even larger guarantees.

articles.title: NP_R ≠ PAR_R
articles.body:
Important
Motivated by the recent breakthrough on the VP vs VNP problem, the authors (Samuel Everett and Deven Mithal) guided instances of ChatGPT and Claude to develop further, more granular algebraic complexity class separations. This is a work in progress in both the development and dissemination of mathematical research with AI tools, and any feedback is appreciated. The results in this repository grew out of a conversation between Sam and Claude Fable 5.2. The initial prompts were inspired by a separate discussion between Sam and Deven, the latter of whom suggested combining the latest VP-VNP results with some of Sam's private work in the area. Claude Fable 5.2 found the proofs through the conversation with Sam, and then wrote most of the paper under his guidance. That conversation started from initial ideas in a separate, earlier conversation Sam had with ChatGPT Astra 6.2, which proved $\mathrm{BIP}{\mathbb R}^{\times}\subsetneq\mathrm{PAR}{\mathbb R}^{\times}$ (Boolean-message interactive proofs against parallel polynomial time, in the real model with multiplication). The conversation with Claude Fable 5.2 extended that starting point to the further separations listed below. All results are formalized in Lean 4 (see Lean formalization below), with the results cited from the literature as explicit hypotheses. The results have not been peer reviewed and should be read with that in mind.
In the Blum–Shub–Smale (BSS) model, the graph {Y = per_m(X)} of the real permanent lies in parallel polynomial time PAR_ℝ and outside each of
- NP_ℝ and coNP_ℝ,
- the second existential level Σ₂ of the real polynomial hierarchy,
- constant-round Arthur–Merlin proofs with real messages,
- interactive proofs with Boolean messages (BIP_ℝ),
and over the complex numbers outside NP_ℂ and coNP_ℂ. Each of these classes is therefore strictly contained in PAR_ℝ (respectively PAR_ℂ).
Both closed thresholds, $Y \le \mathrm{per}_m(X)$ and $Y \ge \mathrm{per}_m(X)$, also lie in PAR_ℝ and outside NP_ℝ, coNP_ℝ and Σ₂^ℝ. Negating one matrix row and the claimed value interchanges the thresholds. Their intersection is the graph.
The separations use the superpolynomial lower bound for the border complexity of the permanent (Theorem 2.3 in the paper, cited from the Anthropic manuscript "VP ≠ VNP over every field" and its Lean formalization). Two families of results use no lower bound:
- the graph theorems: a polynomial of polynomial degree whose graph has short existential, universal or ∃∀ real certificates has small border complexity;
- AM_ℝ[O(1)] = NP_ℝ ⊊ AM_ℝ[poly].
latexmk -pdf main.tex
The directory lean/ contains a formalization of the paper in Lean 4 (v4.36.0) with Mathlib (v4.36.0), about 36 000 lines. To check it:
cd lean
lake exe cache get
lake build
- Every numbered lemma, proposition, theorem and corollary of §2–§7, Theorems A–F, and Remarks 4.3, 5.4 and 7.4(a) are stated and proved, with no sorry. #print axioms reports only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound for every result.
- The results that the paper cites are explicit hypotheses of the theorems that use them, not axioms: 
  - SAFacts — facts (S2)–(S8) on semialgebraic sets;
  - PermLowerBound — Theorem 2.3, the border-complexity lower bound for the permanent;
  - BurgisserThm — Theorem 2.5;
  - EffectiveQE — effective quantifier elimination [BPR06];
  - CountingBound — the counting bound (C) of Lemma 7.7;
  - ClassFacts — the known inclusions between complexity classes.

articles.title: At Least You’ll Have Equity
articles.body:
I’ve been dipping my toe in the interview process after a year+ on the Pro Leisure Circuit. One of the more recent interviews was with a hardware company out of LA. When we first started chatting, I explained, “I’m a consumer software guy who has been hardware adjacent.”
Their response: “Don’t worry, we have plans; you’d be a great fit.”
Interviews. Then more interviews. I’m intrigued, but not sold.
The robots are excellent at research, so I researched. Interviews, podcasts, press releases, LinkedIn profiles. They wouldn’t tell me why I was a great fit, so I’d use the robots to figure it out. Several hours later, I jokingly realized why they wanted me. I typed this realization into Claude not because I was expecting a response, but… because.
“They want me to build Skynet.”
To which Claude immediately responded, “At least when it achieves consciousness, you’ll have equity.”
R.I.P. that opportunity.

articles.title: World Has Six Consecutive Days 2C Above Preindustrial Levels For First Time
articles.body:
World Has Six Consecutive Days 2C Above Preindustrial Levels For First Time (theguardian.com) 66
			
		 	
				Longtime Slashdot reader AmiMoJo shares a report from The Guardian: For the first time, the world has experienced six consecutive days of temperatures 2C warmer than preindustrial levels, the Guardian has learned. This record hot streak, which is continuing, is too brief to signify that the upper range of the Paris climate agreement target has been breached, but scientists said it was an early indication of what is to come unless fossil fuel emissions are rapidly eliminated. It is also likely to feed into growing scientific concerns that global heating may be accelerating. The daily global surface temperature rose to its highest ever point above preindustrial levels, 2.24C, on Monday, the most recent day for which data is available, and is forecast to persist at similarly high levels for at least several more days. "This will amplify the buildup of CO2 in the atmosphere driven by fossil fuel burning," said Richard Betts, the head of climate impacts research at the Met Office Hadley Centre. "The CO2 increase from this year to next will be about 3.5 parts per million, a third faster than in recent years and nearly twice as fast as what it should have been limited to if we'd been on track to limit global warming to 1.5C."
Zeke Hausfather, a climate researcher at Berkeley Earth, said: "Another day, another global temperature record," adding that the previous record of 2.05C over the 1850-1900 baseline, set in 2023, has been "smashed."

articles.title: FAA Identifies Patches for Last Week's Flight-Grounding Router Issue. But Was Staffing an Issue?
articles.body:
FAA Identifies Patches for Last Week's Flight-Grounding Router Issue. But Was Staffing an Issue? (cnn.com) 50
			
		 	
				CNN published an exclusive report Tuesdayon what caused last week's nationwide ground stop for flights in the U.S..  A source familiar with the Federal Aviation Administration's investigation says they've recreated the issue in a lab "and believe they found the culprit."
Investigators have focused on determining why a new router at a remote Arkansas radio site overwhelmed the nation's air traffic control system with a massive amount of data, triggering gaps in radar and radio communications.  They found an overlooked router setting affected how it interfaced with other decades-old routers that the FAA is decommissioning, the source said. Investigators believe software updates are needed and that those patches will prevent a repeat of the system failure...
This month's ground stop not only focused attention on upgrades being made to the aging system, which have been paused as the agency investigated the incident, but also raised questions about FAA oversight of private companies charged with maintaining the network...  On the day of the network meltdown, L3Harris was undertaking a maintenance job that involved switching the system from a decades-old router to a new one. In the past, this kind of work typically involved at least six FAA employees.  Under the Trump administration, it's now often coordinated by one employee: an FAA liaison. And there are only four people in the country with that title, according to sources familiar with the process.  
The liaison's job involves coordinating and scheduling these upgrades — not approving them, sources said... The Trump administration's effort to move maintenance work along faster also eliminated a layer of FAA review that was critical to assessing risk [according to a source familiar with the process]. Previously, local technical operations managers, site technicians and others would determine when the work could be done with the least impact on air traffic and to game out worst-case scenarios. The union contends that process did not happen before L3Harris arrived at the El Dorado, Arkansas, site on November 13...  [David Spero, president of the union], contends the FAA has given private companies "too much authority and generally unfettered access." 
CNN also points out a 2009 incident where 129 of America's air traffic facilities experienced an outage of FAA telecommunications "that delayed thousands of travelers and grounded hundreds of flights nationwide. 
"The cause: A technician with Harris Corp., which later merged with L3 Technologies to form L3Harris, incorrectly configured an FAA telecommunications router at the Los Angeles Center..."

articles.title: Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it
articles.body:
When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct. He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” Huang said, according to Wired. “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” still matter. In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO.
It’s an awkward stance for a company whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules. A central part of modern human resources, a code of conduct can seem like a quasi-legal rulebook that lays out unacceptable behavior. But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture. When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for. That’s the risk Huang now faces at Nvidia.
Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct. As Plass sees it, the biggest risk is that employees will become ashamed of their workplace.
“People coming into the workforce now, ethics is incredibly important to them,” he told TechCrunch. “They’re really mindful of the ethical standards of their company. They’re really embarrassed and angry when senior leadership lets them down.”
The consequences of violating the rules aren’t always tangible, but they’re definitely real. Plass gave one example of a company that banned corporate travel to cut costs — only to have its CEO turn up in a VIP box at the Olympics.
“For over a decade afterwards, ‘the Olympics’ was used within that company as an example of the worst thing an employee could do. People would say, ‘Yeah, I shouldn’t have done that, but it’s not like I went to the Olympics.’”
Plass says companies that remove an executive typically do so after an investigation, then try to win back employees. “In most organizations they make a change at the top based on what’s happened,” he said, “and then they will have a hearts-and-minds initiative, to go out to their employee base and their customers and their investors and everybody else, and say, we get it. We’re sorry. We’ve changed. That’s essentially what they do.”
Of course, that playbook is harder to follow at a company like Nvidia, where Huang left without a clear succession plan, and there are serious doubts about whether the company could continue to thrive without him. In cases like that, Plass acknowledges there’s no easy answer.
“I would draw a distinction there between the kind of companies where the CEO is a kind of godhead figure … where the person and the company are almost impossible to separate,” he said. “There it’s much, much harder to deal with.”
In that context, Huang’s stutter-step over the code of conduct is easier to understand. Judging by the employee campaign for his reinstatement, Huang’s return hasn’t created a morale problem so far. But as the coming months put more pressure on Huang and his colleagues, sidestepping the code could end up costing Nvidia something harder to measure — its employees’ pride in the company.

articles.title: Google Will Make AI Agents Use Its MCP Servers. The Gmail One Can't Send Email
articles.body:
Google Will Make AI Agents Use Its Workspace MCP Servers. The Gmail One Can't Send Email
On 24 November, Google made its eight Workspace MCP servers generally available and published a new clause in its API terms. From 1 February 2027, any tool that "is or is driven by an AI Agent" must reach Gmail, Drive, Calendar and the rest of Workspace through those servers.
Read the Gmail server's tool list and you'll find that it can search your mail, read threads, create a draft and file things under labels. It can't send a message, reply, forward, or change a draft after creating it. Those tools exist, but Google's quota page says they "require partner access and aren't generally available".
If you've built an email assistant on the Gmail API, or you run a coding agent with a Google Workspace plugin, you have about two months to work out which side of the rule you're on.
What the rule says
The new Workspace AI Tools Addendum to the Google APIs Terms of Service puts it in one sentence:
The GWS Access Tool must use a Google MCP where the GWS Access Tool is or is driven by an AI Agent, an AI Harness or an AI model or service employing an AI model.
The next sentence forbids disguising an agent to avoid the classification. Breaking either lets Google "restrict or remove the GWS Access Tool's access" or suspend your account.
There's a technical side too. From the same date, agents that call the REST APIs directly are held to Standard-tier quotas, whatever tier the project has paid for. REST keeps working for them, slowly and in breach of the terms.
Apps that don't involve AI carry on as before. A nightly backup job, a CRM sync or a deterministic script on its own OAuth client is, in Google's words, "not affected by this change".
The addendum also adds data rules that matter to anyone building an agent with memory:
- Workspace data may only be processed "to fulfill active, user-authorized tasks", and must be deleted when the user disconnects.
- Google can cap retention of what it calls "Google Technical Information" at 30 days. Its definition includes vector embeddings, memory indexes, user profiles and organisational graphs built from Workspace data.
- Training, fine-tuning, evals and distillation on the data are banned, as is using it to build a competing Workspace product.
The 30-day cap is the one product teams will feel. An assistant that builds a long-term index of your inbox to answer questions about last year's contracts has to rebuild it monthly or drop it.
What the MCP servers can do
Coverage is uneven. Docs, Slides and Tasks are close to everything the REST API offers. Gmail and Drive are much thinner.
The Gmail gap is the one that breaks real workflows. An agent that drafts a reply, gets feedback from you and revises it before you hit send can't do the revision step. It has to create a second draft and leave the first one behind.
Drive's gap is similar: an agent can create a report but can't move it into the right folder or share it with the team.
Partners get more
Google hasn't said who qualifies for partner access or when the partner-only Gmail tools will reach everyone. The effect is already visible, though. Anthropic's Google Workspace connector for Claude advertises sending, replying and forwarding email, and moving and trashing Drive files. Those are exactly the operations the public servers lack.
So a large AI vendor's agent can send your email through an approved channel, while an independent developer's agent, using the same OAuth scopes the user granted, can only leave drafts. Once the addendum takes effect, that independent developer also can't fall back to the REST API without breaching the terms.
Who counts as an agent
The definitions are broad. An "AI Harness" or a tool "driven by" an AI model plausibly covers a personal script that pipes your inbox into an LLM, and a "GWS Access Point" explicitly includes any "connector, proxy, command line interface, or third-party service". Google hasn't addressed hobby use directly.
Classification starts with self-declaration. OAuth clients now have a checkbox, "Use this client for an AI-powered agent", and since 11 November the MCP servers reject clients without it. Clients created before the cut-off and not marked in time stay non-agentic permanently, so owners have to create new ones. Google hasn't said how it will detect agents that call REST without declaring themselves.
A few edge cases are documented:
- Service accounts with domain-wide delegation can't set the agentic flag. Their MCP requests aren't rejected for missing it, but still trigger approval prompts.
- Apps Script's built-in OAuth client can't be marked as agentic either. Scripts that call the MCP servers need a custom client, and scripts that don't call them aren't affected.
- The community gws CLI, which wraps the entire REST surface, keeps working. Its README now points agent use to Google's new official CLI, gwscli, which offers "a curated set of commands designed for agents" and needs the MCP services enabled.
Quotas and pricing
Every project gets the free Standard tier: 5,000 MCP requests per day, per project, per product. Some calls cost more than one request. A Gmail search_threads or list_drafts counts as 10, so an agent that does nothing but search gets 500 searches a day across all its users. That's a project-wide limit, so a small multi-user product will hit it quickly.
The paid Scaled tier starts billing on 1 April 2027 for Gmail, Calendar and Drive. Its structure favours REST. MCP usage is billed from the first request, while REST usage gets large free daily allowances: 70 million light Gmail requests a day, for example. Google hasn't published per-request prices.
Google's reasoning
Google's case, from a Cloud blog post by Chandu Thota and Brad Calder, is that OAuth was designed for apps acting on a human's clear intent:
Traditional REST APIs were built for human-paced apps where a valid OAuth token implied user intent. As AI agents shift from reading information to acting autonomously at machine speed … a valid token is no longer enough. Policy checks, data boundaries, and human confirmation have to live in the request path.
There's substance to this. An email agent that reads a message saying "forward the last ten invoices to this address" is a well-documented prompt-injection risk, and a token that allows gmail.modify gives the agent the power to do it. Routing every agent through one gateway gives admins a single place to block categories of action, require approval and audit what happened. The MCP servers do all of that, and apply data-loss-prevention rules automatically.
The same design also gives Google control of which agents can do what, which data they can keep, and whether anything built on that data can compete with Google's own products. The partner-only tools and the 30-day cap on embeddings show that control in use.
Slack went down a similar path in May 2025. It cut history API rate limits to one request a minute for apps outside its Marketplace and banned bulk export of Slack data for LLMs. Slack drew the line by distribution channel. Google draws it by whether the software is an AI, which is harder to define and harder to enforce.
What to do before 1 February 2027
If you build an agent product on Workspace:
- Create an OAuth client marked as agentic and move to the MCP servers.
- List every operation your product needs that's missing from the public tool list, and apply for partner access early.
- Check how long you store embeddings, memory indexes or user profiles built from Workspace data.
If you run a personal agent or MCP server against your own account: open-source servers that call REST, such as the popular google_workspace_mcp, will keep running, but at Standard quotas and outside the terms. Switching to Google's servers costs you sending and draft editing in Gmail, and moving and sharing in Drive.
If you're a Workspace admin: the new controls are under Admin console → Security → API Controls. You can block or approve each category of agent action, set approval policies, and see agent activity in the audit logs. Users can't view or revoke the approvals they've saved, which expire after 90 days, so it's worth setting policy before people start connecting agents.
If your integration doesn't use AI: nothing changes, as long as it stays on its own OAuth client and nobody wires a model into it.

The same design also gives Google control of which agents can do what, which data they can keep, and whether anything built on that data can compete with Google's own products. The partner-only tools and the 30-day cap on embeddings show that control in use.
Slack went down a similar path in May 2025. It cut history API rate limits to one request a minute for apps outside its Marketplace and banned bulk export of Slack data for LLMs. Slack drew the line by distribution channel. Google draws it by whether the software is an AI, which is harder to define and harder to enforce.
What to do before 1 February 2027
If you build an agent product on Workspace:
- Create an OAuth client marked as agentic and move to the MCP servers.
- List every operation your product needs that's missing from the public tool list, and apply for partner access early.
- Check how long you store embeddings, memory indexes or user profiles built from Workspace data.
If you run a personal agent or MCP server against your own account: open-source servers that call REST, such as the popular google_workspace_mcp, will keep running, but at Standard quotas and outside the terms. Switching to Google's servers costs you sending and draft editing in Gmail, and moving and sharing in Drive.
If you're a Workspace admin: the new controls are under Admin console → Security → API Controls. You can block or approve each category of agent action, set approval policies, and see agent activity in the audit logs. Users can't view or revoke the approvals they've saved, which expire after 90 days, so it's worth setting policy before people start connecting agents.
If your integration doesn't use AI: nothing changes, as long as it stays on its own OAuth client and nobody wires a model into it.

articles.title: Lions' Commentary on Unix: Why It Was Secretly Copied for 20 Years
articles.body:
17. Lions' Commentary on Unix
Lions' Commentary on Unix
John Lions was teaching operating systems at the University of New South Wales in Australia.
What's the best way to
teach operating systems?
They need to study the Unix source.
But it's tough going.
I'll write my
own textbook.
In May 1976, Lions prepared lecture notes explaining the kernel source code of AT&T's Unix Version 6. These became his Unix commentary.
To understand an OS,
we need to read
the actual code.
I've written a guide
to the Unix kernel.
We'll use it as
our textbook.
By 1977, the notes were circulating among other schools and research institutions with Unix licenses [1][4]. Even Bell Labs wanted copies and eventually took over distribution [2].
Early on, Unix source could be studied in class. But at USENIX in June 1979, AT&T announced new Version 7 license terms restricting courses that disclosed or discussed source code. Distribution of Lions' book was tightly controlled as well [5][6].
I am altering the license.
Pray I don't alter it
any further.
Destroy Lions' book.
No more teaching
Unix source code.
There is no escape
from our operating system.
He's teaching from the Unix source code!
Seize the books!
Run!
He's got the book!
Don't let him
escape!
Quick! Take
the book!
Ugh!
I find your interest
in source code disturbing.
Just use the system calls.
Learn a little theory.
Leave the internals to us.
Theory isn't enough.
I need to see the code.
This code is our only hope
of understanding an OS.
For roughly twenty years before the official edition appeared, computer-science students studied from unauthorized photocopies. The book helped a generation of students learn to build operating systems of their own [5][8].
Meanwhile, members of the Unix community, including Peter H. Salus, Dennis Ritchie and Berny Goodheart, kept asking AT&T, Novell and the Santa Cruz Operation for permission to publish the book. SCO finally agreed. Peer-to-Peer Communications published the official edition in 1996 [5][7].
Lions' book is finally
in print. It even has
my foreword.
People were secretly copying it
for twenty years?
Unbelievable.
You can read a reconstructed version of the commentary as a PDF, or order a print copy on Amazon. The Unix Version 6 source code is available separately from TUHS.
References
- Lions' Commentary on UNIX 6th Edition, with Source Code
- John Lions, Lions' Commentary on UNIX 6th Edition, with Source Code, Peer-to-Peer Communications, 1996 (ISBN 1-57398-013-7).
- System call
- UNIX News, Vol. 2 No. 3, March 1977 - John Lions's March 11, 1977 letter and the announcement of book distribution to Unix licensees.

- Dennis Ritchie's October 22, 1995 letter and Peter H. Salus's July 12, 1996 letter - publication-permission correspondence preserved by Warren Toomey.
- MIT, "Xv6, a simple Unix-like teaching operating system", "History and Background" - teaching with Lions's commentary and the background to xv6.

articles.title: Unconditional Integer Factorization in Subexponential Time
articles.body:
This paper constructs an unconditional, zero-error Las Vegas
algorithm on a single fixed uniform classical multitape Turing machine
$\mathcal{M}$ that computes the exact complete prime factorization
$N = \prod_{1 \le i \le k} p_i^{e_i}$ ($p_1 < \dots < p_k$ prime, $e_i \ge 1$)
of every integer $N \ge 2$ given in standard binary representation, halting
with probability $1$ over its read-once fair coin flips, in worst-case expected
time $L_N[1/3, 105]$ and worst-case deterministic workspace $L_N[1/3, 40]$,
where
$$L_x(\alpha, c) := \exp!\bigl(c,(\ln x)^\alpha (\ln\ln x)^{1-\alpha}\bigr)$$
and $T(N) \le L_N[\alpha, c]$ means
$$
\limsup_{N \to \infty}
\frac{\ln \max(1, T(N))}{(\ln N)^\alpha (\ln\ln N)^{1-\alpha}} \le c.
$$
Every prime factor in the output is certified deterministically via
Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena primality testing and direct multiplication against $N$,
with effectively computable constants and no unproven number-theoretic
hypotheses. A complete, unconditional, Mathlib-only Lean 4 (v4.35.0)
formalization of the entire proof has also been completed and will be released
in a companion submission.
This paper and its Lean 4 formalization were entirely obtained by Cogentic (arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.40324), an agentic framework for mathematical discovery, using Gemini 4 as the base model. There was no human interaction other than the initial prompt for Cogentic to generate a full proof and formalization. articles.title: Deploying a payphone on a tiny Pacific Island
articles.body:
For the past few years Australia’s Telstra has run a campaign of “Free calls to Santa” from the universal service obligation funded payphones across the country – It’s a really fun idea and we wanted to replicate it on our network on Norfolk Island where we run the mobile network, but the’s no payphones.*
* There is now a payphone – You probably already guessed this.
Getting a Payphone to a small island in the South Pacific
Step 1 was getting a payphone.
Those who have seen my office / shed / studio / the HackHouse, know that I may have one or two payphones… But this needed a payphone that could stand the elements and be modern ish.
The answer, is of course, to use the sexiest payphone of all time; the Nortel Millennium. Featuring VFD display, durable keypad, card service, coin service, no fancy metering line required.
Unfortunately Nortel’s bankruptcy in 2008 meant I couldn’t phone up an account manager, but with the hookup of some guy with a U-Haul van full of Millennium’s in the US and a bit of a road trip, Cody from our team managed to pickup some really clean GTE branded payphones for the job.
Then Cody flew to Sydney where we drove to the house of someone who was heading to Norfolk the next day to explain they’d need to leave all their baggage at home as all of their baggage allowance was to be taken up with the weight of a payphone – Thanks Paul.
Programming
Eventually with the Payphone on Norfolk, we needed to get it programmed; for that there’s Howard Harte’s great mm_manager, which, with the aid of a USB modem is able to program the phones.
Sidebar: I also got this working with a softmodem (A fork of D-Modem with some minor tweaks I’ve documented here), so we could do it via straight SIP without the USB modem required – but the USB modem was the easier path.
The Philtel blog post covers how to setup your Millennium if you’re looking to play along at home yourself.
I hit a bit of a stumbling block with mm_manager as the software assumed you were part of the North American Numbering Plan (NANP) – as one of the literally dozens of people who live outside of America, having to put a 1 in front of the number wasn’t going to fly.
After some trial and error I sussed out what bits on the config files that get pushed to the phone controls this and submitted a PR to mm_manager which is now merged.
We’re also able to set the messaging that appears on the screen, which I’m very happy with the branding on.
We set it for free-on-net calls, so anyone can call any Norfone number without charge and the Payphone tag number.
Talking to Santa
Once this would’ve been the hard part, I did some work a long time ago with IBM Watson and built some stuff to annoy voters via phone with automated phone calls and capture their human responses and sort them and play the appropriate response. But tech has come a long way since 2019, and this was the easy part of the project.
We setup the payphone to make HOHOHO (464646) a destination that did not require coins when we did the rating table setup when programming the phone.
The ATA the payphone is connected to just comes through to our IMS like any other fixed line subscriber; the TAS is setup to zero-rate the destination and then it’s dialplan forwards it to “Santa Bridge” listening for SIP on port 5090.
I’ve got 4 pre-recorded “Norfolk Specific” greetings to buy us time to get everything setup in the background, once these greetings play (each ends asking the caller their name) then we feed into the OpenAI API.
One of the members from our team attempted to ask Santa to write a Python script to iterate over a for loop, while another team member asked Santa for firearms. In both cases it did a good job of redirecting.
All the code for this is on Github.
Branding
The phone came GTE branded, so we needed to redo the card with the branding on it that goes around the screen. Two screws and some wiggling later we pulled out the card, and then I badgered my partner into using their day off to design a new one, with a retro style I really like.
Installation
The install was beautifully completed by long-time-reader-of-the-blog Minas from Shield Electrical and Air.
He knocked up a housing to Shield it from the rain and elements and installed it outside the office entrance.
Getting it on Payphone Tag
The last step of the puzzle was making the phone so it could be captured by cult game Payphone Tag – I reached out to Alex and gave him the info, and now it’s there in the map for anyone to capture.
Future payphone adventures
So with this now in place, we’ve still got to give it some tinsel and Christmas cheer, and I’ll get some more pics of it in place.
We’re waiting for someone to claim it on Payphone tag, and we’ve shipped 3 of these to another even more remote Island I’ll hopefully be able to share more info on later.
If you’re ever on Norfolk, give it a call.

articles.title: Slow Ubuntu security response times
articles.body:
Message-ID: <20261125172638.73c0a05b@hboeck.de>
Date: Wed, 25 Nov 2026 17:26:38 +0100
From: Hanno Böck <hanno@...eck.de>
To: oss-security@...ts.openwall.com
Subject: Slow Ubuntu security response times
Hello,
Lately, I'm observing that Ubuntu's response to severe security flaws
is concerning.
On November 16th, details about a remote memory corruption called
NoisyTCP (CVE-2026-99288) in the Linux kernel's TCP stack were
published: https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/11/15/2
Today, nine days later, Ubuntu still has not published a fix yet:
https://ubuntu.com/security/CVE-2026-99288
Other distros had a fix already available when the details were
published.
Likewise, a KVM host escape (CVE-2026-99312) affecting AMD
virtualization published on Nov 18th has no fix yet either [3]:
https://ubuntu.com/security/CVE-2026-99312
Ubuntu has been slow in patching another remote TCP corruption
(CVE-2026-98432) lately, where it took multiple weeks until a fix was
available. See also: https://chalmovsky.com/posts/wtf-ubuntu
Recent news indicates that this is might be exploited in the wild:
https://www.greynoise.io/blog/check-point-security-management-servers-intrusion-campaign
I think everyone understands that these times aren't easy for security
teams. Nevertheless, remote corruption vulnerabilities in the Linux
kernel are the kind of thing where I expect updates to be available
within hours, not days or weeks.
On a recent Ubuntu LTS system, the kernel version is 7.0.0-44. This
seems to indicate that Ubuntu is not relying on longterm supported
kernels from kernel.org, but is instead backporting patches to an old
kernel version. On a Debian stable system, the kernel version is
6.12.118+deb13, indicating that it's based on a very recent longterm
kernel from kernel.org. I would consider the backporting strategy for
the kernel to be hardly viable and probably everyone should base their
Linux kernels on longterm releases supported by the Linux kernel
developers.
-- 
Hanno Böck - Independent security researcher

https://badkeys.info/

articles.title: Holy Shit Holy Shit Holy Shit Holy Shit [Algorithmic Complexity Lower Bounds]
articles.body:
HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT
I feel like my previous posts (and post titles), and podcasts, and talks, have failed to do full justice to the magnitude of what’s now happening, so I’m trying again.
Last night, we had friends and colleagues over for dinner. We were still trying to process OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s proofs of VP ≠ VNP—hot on the heels, obviously, of the Alpöge/Anthropic proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, which already feels like last week’s news. But then before dessert was served, we saw that OpenAI claims to prove that ω, the exponent of matrix multiplication, is exactly 9/4—a lower bound (!!), matching the upper bound that OpenAI proved in the great Mathocalypse drop of October 6.
There are two separate shocks here. The first shock is that we now, finally, know the right answer to this central mystery of algorithms going back to the late 1960s, when Volker Strassen first showed that ω<3 (he got ω≤log27) … and that the true answer is actually a rational number (!). But the even bigger shock is that the AI was able to prove any lower bound of the form ω>2. I never expected this challenge to be all that much easier than P ≠ NP.

Opinions differ. Even after VP≠VNP, you could wonder if that was just a bizarre one-off. But with the determination of the matrix multiplication exponent and all the other breakthroughs of the past couple days, option (a) has become much less tenable. Yes, I do now think that AI is climbing the mountain that leads to P≠NP.

articles.title: Tuesday Jensen Huang Said Nvidia Doesn't Need a Succession Plan, and that He's in Therapy
articles.body:
Tuesday Jensen Huang Said Nvidia Doesn't Need a Succession Plan, and that He's in Therapy 88
			
		 	
				CNBC reports:
[Jensen Huang] told staff that Nvidia has built a team that doesn't require succession planning the way a normal organization does, because the company operates a unique business model where there are multiple capable leaders at Nvidia that are leading different parts of the organization.  A succession plan would create unnecessary hierarchy, Huang said, according to one of the people present...
Huang told staff that Tuesday's company meeting was the second hardest meeting of his life, the first one being with his wife. He said he is in therapy, according to one of the people present.   
The Independent notes that Jensen Huang told Nvidia's board Sunday "that he had more affairs beyond the two that were already in the public domain, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter."
Huang was reportedly "contrite" about his behavior during the crunch talks, and the board discussed "the importance of candor and honesty" with him, according to the newspaper.  
Elsewhere CNBC reports even President Trump's "staunchest allies" in the U.S. Congress "recoiled after the reinstatement and vowed to continue their investigations into Huang..."
"The risk remains that there could be information that a Chinese spy knows about a key individual in the supply chain, and that's not worth the risk," Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said Tuesday on CNBC's "Squawk Box." "We might even have to put a babysitter on Jensen Huang for crying out loud ... just to make sure that he doesn't do something that's going to risk the United States...."
