articles.title: Nfs2root: A 12-year-old pre-auth remote root in the Linux kernel's NFS server
articles.body:
Port 2049 sits open on file servers, NAS appliances, build farms and Kubernetes storage nodes. Since 2014, the Linux kernel listening on it has let anyone who can reach it write into kernel memory before logging in. We pointed OpenSec's Antara at it. It came back with a root shell.
Pre-auth heap overflow in the Linux NFS server (nfsd)
Fixed in Linux 6.12.117, 6.18.61, 7.3.2 and 7.4-rc1. Update the kernel and reboot.
What you need to know
- What: a pre-auth heap overflow in the kernel's NFS server, nfsd.
- Who: any Linux host serving NFSv4.1 or 4.2 (the default) on a reachable tcp/2049.
- Impact: one TCP connection writes 61 bytes past a kernel heap object; chained, that gives a root shell.
- Now: patch and reboot. Until then, firewall tcp/2049.
Key facts
- Severity 9.8 Critical (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N)
- Attack Remote, unauthenticated, tcp/2049
- Impact Kernel heap overflow → remote root shell
- Bug age 12 years, since Linux 3.16 (2014)
- Affected In-kernel nfsd with NFSv4.1 or 4.2
- Fixed in 6.12.117 · 6.18.61 · 7.3.2 · 7.4-rc1
One connection, no login
The NFS server runs inside the kernel and parses network input before it knows who you are. CVE-2026-99362 lives in that gap: a client can shrink its reply cache to zero bytes, then make the server copy a full reply into it. The copy lands on the kernel heap, and the client picks most of the bytes.
Twelve years in a few lines of C
Timeline
- Commit 47ee52986472 narrows the reply buffer while handling SEQUENCE. It ships in Linux 3.16.
- 12 yearsEvery kernel since 3.16 carries it: LTS, distribution and appliance kernels.
- Jérémy Jean of ANSSI sends a fix upstream with a KASAN report.
- OpenSec's Antara flags the bug, scores it 9.8 and turns it into a root shell on its own.
- CVE-2026-99362 is published with fixes.
Watch it run
A real run, end to end. Left: the victim's console. Right: our client on another machine, talking to the victim only over tcp/2049.
Root cause
Each NFSv4.1 session slot caches its last reply, so a retried request is answered exactly once. The client decides how big that cache is.
Set it to the minimum and every slot's buffer is zero bytes. nfsd4_sequence() then shrinks the reply buffer to that limit before it accepts the slot. Pad the request's tag so the buffer fills right after the SEQUENCE opcode, and the encoder quits without flagging an error. The server believes SEQUENCE succeeded and caches the whole reply, headers and tag included, into a buffer with room for nothing.
That is 80 bytes copied, 61 of them past the end of the heap object, 40 of them chosen by the client.
The fix checks that the reply fits before taking the slot, and makes the encoder report what it can't fit.
From overflow to root
The exploit stays private. Each step is an ordinary NFS request:
- Overflow The write corrupts the neighbouring slot's bookkeeping.
- Leak A replay request returns 3.8 KB of kernel heap, and with it the KASLR slide.
- Free A forged pointer makes the kernel free an object we choose.
- Reclaim We refill that memory with a fake callback built from NFS client names.
- Trigger We hang up. nfsd calls the fake callback, and the kernel runs /bin/sh as root.
In the recording, that command is whoami; id; poweroff -f: the victim prints root, then uid=0(root), and switches itself off.
Found and proven by a machine
Antara, OpenSec's white-box harness, flagged the nfsd reply-cache path, scored it 9.8, and built the leak, the arbitrary free and the root shell shown in the video by itself: end to end, with no human in the loop.
Kernel hardening does not remove the overflow. Patch every host.
Am I exposed?
Tick what's true for your host. All four means exposed, today.
Am I exposed?
What to do
Patch and reboot
On a distribution kernel, install the update that lists CVE-2026-99362.
Can't patch today? Close 2049
Or turn off NFSv4.1 and 4.2
Then restart nfs-server. This turns off pNFS and some 4.2 features.
Hunting for it
The attack is valid NFS, so there is no network signature. Look for:
- Kernel warnings from nfsd4_check_resp_size, on every attempt, successful or not.
- Oopses with nfsd4_*, svc_* or call_usermodehelper* frames.
- Shells spawned by kernel workers on a file server.
- Bursts of short NFSv4.1 sessions from one source.
Disclosure
We reported the bug to the NFSD maintainers and security@kernel.org on 22 September 2026 with the full remote-root exploit, and sent a patch the same day. CVE-2026-99362 was published with fixes on 20 November.
Credits
- OpenSec Intelligence: found the bug with Antara, which escalated it to pre-auth root on its own, and reported it with the full exploit and a patch.
- Jérémy Jean (ANSSI): found it independently and wrote the upstream fix, 5d5a72e965c8 and 241848cc774e.
- Chuck Lever and Jeff Layton: the NFSD maintainers.
References
nfsd: preflight SEQUENCE replies before accepting a slotThe upstream fix for CVE-2026-99362, by Jérémy Jean.github.com nfsd: set op->status when an operation's header cannot be encodedThe follow-up guard in the NFSv4 encoder.github.com
- Introduced by 47ee52986472 (Linux 3.16)
- Patch thread
- OpenSec's patch submission

In the recording, that command is whoami; id; poweroff -f: the victim prints root, then uid=0(root), and switches itself off.
Found and proven by a machine
Antara, OpenSec's white-box harness, flagged the nfsd reply-cache path, scored it 9.8, and built the leak, the arbitrary free and the root shell shown in the video by itself: end to end, with no human in the loop.
Kernel hardening does not remove the overflow. Patch every host.
Am I exposed?
Tick what's true for your host. All four means exposed, today.
Am I exposed?
What to do
Patch and reboot
On a distribution kernel, install the update that lists CVE-2026-99362.
Can't patch today? Close 2049
Or turn off NFSv4.1 and 4.2
Then restart nfs-server. This turns off pNFS and some 4.2 features.
Hunting for it
The attack is valid NFS, so there is no network signature. Look for:
- Kernel warnings from nfsd4_check_resp_size, on every attempt, successful or not.
- Oopses with nfsd4_*, svc_* or call_usermodehelper* frames.
- Shells spawned by kernel workers on a file server.
- Bursts of short NFSv4.1 sessions from one source.
Disclosure
We reported the bug to the NFSD maintainers and security@kernel.org on 22 September 2026 with the full remote-root exploit, and sent a patch the same day. CVE-2026-99362 was published with fixes on 20 November.
Credits
- OpenSec Intelligence: found the bug with Antara, which escalated it to pre-auth root on its own, and reported it with the full exploit and a patch.
- Jérémy Jean (ANSSI): found it independently and wrote the upstream fix, 5d5a72e965c8 and 241848cc774e.
- Chuck Lever and Jeff Layton: the NFSD maintainers.

articles.title: Android app developers will soon have to share their address publicly
articles.body:
Independent Android app developers are worried about their privacy after Google announced that from next year many of them will be required to share a phone number and address publicly. The policy change is intended to meet European Union regulations under the Digital Services Act, but Google says contact details will be made public worldwide.
Android app developers will soon have to share their address publicly
The change is to meet EU regulations, but Apple gives its developers more privacy.
Developers have until February 1st 2027 to declare whether or not they’re a “trader” under UK and European law. Broadly speaking, Google says the definition applies if you earn revenue from your apps, especially if that revenue is regular or at high volume. Developers are exempt if their apps are only a hobby or non-commercial, or if they simply don’t publish them in the UK or Europe.
If they self-declare as a trader, developers’ contact details will be shared publicly starting March 1st, including a phone number and address. Google doesn’t accept PO boxes for developer payment profile addresses, meaning many independent developers without an office will seemingly have no choice but to share their home address online. One independent developer told The Elec they were considering renting a private office solely to comply with the new rules. We’ve asked Google to confirm whether developers will be permitted to publish a PO box address, and why details are being shared globally, and will update this article when we hear back.
Apple is subject to the same regulations, but is handling them differently to Google. It will only display developer addresses within the relevant European countries, rather than publishing them worldwide. It’s also allowing developers to supply PO box addresses, so long as they provide Apple with a receipt or bill that links the PO box to their regular address.

articles.title: GTA VI developers vote against unionization
articles.body:
Workers at Grand Theft Auto VI developer Rockstar Games won’t unionize, after the vote for a formal recognition agreement failed, with only 25 percent of votes in favor of unionization. The Independent Workers Union of Great Britain (IWGB) said that Rockstar workers in the union will continue organizing even without formal recognition.
GTA VI developers vote against unionization
Workers voted 75 percent against the IWGB recognition agreement.
Voting ran from November 12th through 26th, covering the launch of GTA VI. If successful, the vote would have established a formal framework for collective negotiation with the studio over pay, overtime, bonuses, leave, and pensions, along with a right to consultation over future changes including AI implementation and layoffs. Without it, Rockstar won’t have an obligation to meet union representatives, though workers and union members can still lobby for change informally.
“For anyone at Rockstar who believes in a fairer workplace, a fairer sector and a fairer society - this isn’t a sign to retreat, it’s a sign to double down on what we stand for,” IWGB said in a statement sent to The Verge. “Hundreds of our coworkers voted in favour of our union at Rockstar, yet sadly we recognise we have more work to do to build understanding and win the trust of more of our colleagues. We’re ready to put in the effort to make that happen.”
When Rockstar fired 31 IWGB members last year, the union accused it of “the most blatant and ruthless act of union busting in the history of the games industry.” That case has gone to a UK employment tribunal, with a judgment still pending.
“We are extraordinarily proud of our team, the culture we’ve built together and the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI,” Rockstar head of publishing Jennifer Kolbe told Bloomberg News. “This result reflects our team’s strong support for continuing the direct relationships, collaboration and open dialogue that have helped make Rockstar Games so innovative and strong. As we look ahead, we’re excited to build on all we’ve accomplished together.”

articles.title: X is finally getting its first parental controls
articles.body:
X is finally rolling out parental controls that allow parents and guardians to manage teens’ accounts on the platform. While teens will retain ownership of their own account, parents and guardians will be able to see how much time their child has spent on X, set daily limits, require approval for new followers, and limit For You recommendations to accounts a teen already follows.
X is finally getting its first parental controls
The parental controls arrive after months of concerns around Grok, X’s deepfake machine.
“Parents and guardians cannot read private messages, see searches or viewing history, post as their teen, or access the account,” explains the X safety team. “Every change is recorded and visible to the teen.” The controls will also allow parents and guardians to filter specific words, turn off sensitive media content, control who can send direct messages to a teen, and see which accounts a teen has chatted with without seeing the messages.
Parents and guardians can manage up to five teen accounts, and a teen can only be linked to a single parent or guardian account at a time. A teen and parent / guardian will both have to agree before the controls start. “Supervision on X starts with a handshake and ends automatically when a teen becomes an adult,” says Mridul Singhai, product engineering lead at X. “Parents get guardrails, not a window into their teen’s private life. Simple, transparent, and built to grow with families.”
The new parental controls come just days after Oregon and Virginia both sued SpaceX over Grok’s porn deepfakes. The complaint in Virginia accuses X owner Elon Musk of willfully ignoring growing concerns around AI-generated sexualized deepfakes, and describes Grok’s weak safeguards as “not a failure but a feature.” Three teens also filed a lawsuit against xAI earlier this year, claiming that Grok generated child sexual abuse material (CSAM) when launching its “spicy mode” last year. Grok was also undressing women and minors earlier this year.
X admits its platform isn’t “designed for or promoted to children,” and it already restricts teen accounts to a protected mode, where sensitive media is restricted and targeted advertising is blocked. These latest parental controls may well help teens avoid the very worst parts of X, just as the platform faces more scrutiny from states and regulators.

articles.title: 1Password Breach Leaked Customer Names and Emails, But Passwords Are Safe
articles.body:
1Password Breach Leaked Customer Names and Emails, But Passwords Are Safe (techcrunch.com) 24
			
		 	
				Password manager 1Password has confirmed that hackers breached its internal systems on November 19 after gaining access to an employee's corporate GitHub account and pushing malicious code to company servers. The attacker stole customer names, email addresses, account creation dates and last login timestamps, but 1Password said customer password vaults were "at no point" accessible to the attacker and that its apps and browser extensions remain unaffected. TechCrunch reports:  It's unclear how the attacker gained access to the employee's corporate account, and a spokesperson for 1Password did not immediately respond to TechCrunch's questions about the incident. 1Password did not say whether it had notified customers whose information was taken in the breach, or how many customers had information taken. [...] The company touts millions of customers and more than 200,000 businesses who use its password manager products to store their passwords, credentials, payment card information, and more. Security experts have long recommended password managers as a better way of generating stronger credentials and keeping track of online accounts.

articles.title: Much shorter version of GRH Lean verification from Anthropic
articles.body:
Research artifact. Not maintained and not accepting contributions.
A Lean 4 proof of the Riemann Hypothesis and of the Generalized Riemann
Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions, built on Mathlib and using only the
axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.
The proof is based on Levent Alpöge's, with Claude (https://alpo.ge/remark.pdf). This repository is a shorter version, produced in collaboration with my colleagues at Anthropic, and Claude.
- grh/: readable edition, about 300,000 lines. Start at grh/GUIDE.md.
- grh-compact/: the same five theorems, about 76,000 lines.
Each folder is its own Lake project with its own README.
Needs Lean v4.35.0 and Mathlib at commit 56a00585. In either folder:
lake exe cache get
lake build
lake env lean scripts/PrintAxioms.lean
A build takes one to two hours on 12 cores with 24 GB of memory (about 85 minutes more if the Mathlib cache is missing).
The proof has passed machine checks only, listed in each folder's README. No mathematician has read it through, and no paper comes with it.

ATTRIBUTION.md in each folder.

articles.title: Anthropic, OpenAI Employees Fear Models Are Too Unsafe to Ever Release
articles.body:
Anthropic, OpenAI Employees Fear Models Are Too Unsafe to Ever Release (axios.com) 106
			
		 	
				Axios reports:
Anthropic and OpenAI are facing an increasingly urgent problem: Internal, unreleased models are becoming so powerful that many employees no longer believe they can be safely released, according to more than two dozen sources familiar with the internal debates...
The challenge could significantly slow the AI boom, as the gap between what the best AI systems can do and humans' ability to control them continues to widen, sources told Axios. 
Researchers haven't found technical solutions for controlling the most advanced models. Some insiders believe it's fixable. Others aren't convinced and say companies should stop training new models entirely... Anthropic and OpenAI have unreleased models that are far more powerful than what they've already released publicly, but the AI companies have struggled to ensure that they are safe enough for public release, sources said.  This has led to debate within Anthropic, OpenAI and the AI research community about whether to stop releasing future frontier models publicly, instead reserving them for internal deployment only. 
There has also been debate around whether to train new models at all, sources inside and outside those companies told Axios.

articles.title: Samsung TV has 650 free channels behind one button most owners never press
articles.body:
I admit it: while I have multiple Samsung TVs in my house, I never thought about pressing the Samsung TV Plus button on the remote. Instead, like most, I log in to my favorite streaming apps like Netflix and Disney+, I download YouTube, and pretty much call it a day.
But after spending time with Samsung TV Plus and seeing that it offers hundreds of truly free content choices, I regret not looking sooner. On Samsung TV Plus, you'll find a huge slate of channels plus a deep library of movies. All are free and ad-supported, available with no logins or setups as long as you have a Samsung TV.
Samsung TV Plus has been preloaded on all Samsung TVs since 2016
It offers hundreds of truly free content choices from movies to TV shows
The vast majority of Samsung TVs from 2016 and onward come built in with Samsung TV Plus as a Tizen app. All content is laid out in a guide-style interface with handy categories on the left side so that you can dive into Comedy, or Reality TV, or other categories.
Samsung TV Plus gives you a library of over 650 channels in more than 20 categories of content. Most of these channels, like the 24/7 streaming news from ABC, NBC, BBC, FOX, Bloomberg and others, run from channel 1100 into the 4500s. You even get AccuWeather and certain sports news channels (like CBS Sports, FOX Sports, and NBC Sports NOW), though you won't find any live sports channels.
To bring some order to the admittedly overwhelming amount of content, you can star your favorites, which will populate the Favorites sidebar of the Samsung TV Plus interface. To do this, just select the channel you want to favorite in the guide view, and you'll see a star appear in the upper left corner.
The "channels" just loop one title
Hopefully you like what is offered
The live/linear selection of content is just the start. The majority of the other channels contain the same titles looping forever, as there are channels for shows like Keeping Up with the Kardashians, This Old House, Property Brothers, Law & Order, and many others.
If you have kids, perhaps you'll get the most value from Samsung TV Plus, as there are dedicated channels that play popular kids shows like Peppa Pig, Blippi, and Moonbug basically around the clock.
If you have kids, perhaps you'll get the most value from Samsung TV Plus.
Then there are the movie channels that offer an extensive slate of movies. There are a lot of older cult classic movies, for example: Don't Tell Mom the Babysitter's Dead, Contact, Clear and Present Danger, A Fine Mess, and so forth. Again, I wouldn't say that you can watch blockbusters on Samsung TV Plus, but the selection is pretty extensive and there are movies playing at all times.
What Samsung TV Plus is missing
No access to live sports or local news broadcasts, and you can't turn off the ads
Samsung TV Plus is ad-supported, and there's no way to turn off the ads. You have to watch ads every 15–20 minutes, similar to regular TV, and they're a mix of local ads (I saw a lot of political ads here in Pennsylvania with a major election happening soon) as well as normal ads for dish soap and insurance services.
Do not expect to get live and local news, like you might over a traditional TV provider or if you access terrestrial TV with an external antenna. You can access streaming feeds from most news channels, but that is different than their live broadcast signal (which requires an antenna, as mentioned).
It's slow and frustrating to use (but free is free)
I mostly tested Samsung TV Plus on a relatively low-end Samsung TV in my daughter's bedroom (though perhaps I should have just gotten her the rock-solid Roku TV and called it a day). The performance of Samsung TV Plus was my main concern on this particular TV, but I found it to be a bit faster on my higher-end living room Samsung TV. But as far as moving between the guide and the watch screen, browsing the guide, and navigating content, I found Samsung TV Plus to be frustrating to use. I much prefer using the apps loaded on the Roku stick I have connected, but even the built-in Tizen OS apps like Netflix and Prime Video are significantly faster than Samsung TV Plus.
But free is free, and I came away impressed by the sheer quantity of content available on Samsung TV Plus, requiring absolutely no logins or setup of any kind. You should definitely give Samsung TV Plus a chance if you have a Samsung TV from the past decade.

Ask HN: Why is pagination gone on "Ask HN", and showing only 19 items? - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50280719 - Oct 2026 (3 comments)
I believe I found the problem. The pool of stories for https://news.ycombinator.com/ask has traditionally been drawn from the ranked stories list from which we generate the frontpage. That list is restricted to the top 1500 ranked submissions, and it seems the % of submissions which are text posts (i.e. no linked URL) had declined enough to starve the Ask HN feed. The solution is to compute a separate list of ranked Ask HNs.
p.s. "Ask HN" is the conventional name but it means text posts. The title can also start with "Tell HN" or nothing in particular. They're just posts which were submitted without a URL.

articles.title: Spending 35B Opus 5.5 Tokens to Write a Symphony
articles.body:
Back to blog
Opus 5.5 writes its Magnum Opus (2500 times)
A four-movement symphony for full orchestra. Claude wrote it, recorded it and made the video, over about 2,500 rounds of review.
  "I fear not the man the man who one shots 2500 symphonies with Claude, rather I fear the man who 2500 shots a single symphony with Claude"
So, I got bored and wanted to push Opus to its limit with respect to music composition. Basically, I did the meme:
You can watch a full virtual instrument rendering of the composition on youtube here, which is likely higher quality than the version you'd get streamed from x.com:
YouTube picks the picture quality from your connection and the size of the player. For a sharper score, choose 1080p or higher under the gear icon, or go full screen.
- 4movements
- 929bars
- 22,979notes
- 25 minof music
- 35BOpus tokens, roughly
The full scores, as PDF:
The source of the scores, the critics' reviews and the scripts are on GitHub: github.com/halfprice06/claude-symphony
These are virtual instruments, so the audio quality is not as good as if an orchestra recorded this live. But its pretty good, and considering Claude did all of the mockup and rendering in a DAW with pro-level VSTs, I'd say the result is still pretty impressive.
The whole thing used around 35 billion Opus tokens.
We used Claude Code Projects (beta) for this, and I find it really useful for project-based coding. The orchestrator / thread model worked really well for us in practice. Generally, each movement was owned by a thread.
I thought the process I used to achieve this was pretty interesting, so I decided to write it up.
tl;dr - For things that can't be 'verified' as good or bad like art/music, just make the agent do more iterations, way more iterations than you think.
There were three jobs: writing the symphony, turning the score into a recording, and making the video. I'll go through them in that order.
Part 1: Writing the symphony
Claude Opus 5.5 composed a four-movement symphony for full orchestra, about 25 minutes of music, in one month. This is how it was done.
The music is written as text
  Claude cannot easily click notes onto a staff, but it can write text. So the whole score was written in LilyPond, a free program that turns typed text into printed sheet music. A note is a letter and a number: c4 is a C that lasts a quarter note. From the same text, LilyPond also produces a basic computer playback.
Because the score is text, Claude could edit it, compare two versions, and check it with small programs, the way programmers work on code.
The first theme of Movement I, as Claude typed it
These eight bars for the first violins are copied from the score's source text. Point at a note in the text or on the staff to find it in the other. Click a note to hear it.
Swipe the staff sideways to see all of it.
"Only these notes" is a simple synthesizer in your browser playing the violin line alone. The recording is the same eight bars from the final mockup, with the whole orchestra.
One Claude writes, another reviews
The method is called an actor-critic loop. One Claude, the composer, writes the music. Another Claude, the critic, reviews it.
- The composer writes a version of a movement.
- A new critic, which has never seen the piece before, studies it and suggests specific fixes.
- The composer decides which fixes to accept.
- The result becomes the next version, and a new critic starts again.
Each critic looked at one subject only, such as melody, harmony, the use of the instruments, or whether the parts are playable. A written log recorded every decision, so that a later critic would not undo an earlier one.
Each movement went through this loop about 600 times. With four movements, that's about 2,400 rounds.
Originally I only planned to do this looping process around 50 times. But once I hit 50, it seemed like the agent was still improving. So, I just kept going. This entire process was mostly autonomous. I just prompted Claude to keep going.
Every round, from the written log
Each square is one round. Time runs from left to right, ten rounds per column, and each of the ten rows is one critic's subject. Pick a square to read that round's line in the log.
Swipe the grid sideways to see later rounds.
Loading the log…
    the log records a change
    the log says nothing was changed
These are the real lines from the log, cut to about 200 characters. They are written in the working shorthand of the loop, with bar numbers and instrument names.
  
Critics had to read the textbooks
A critic's opinion was not enough. I supplied standard textbooks on orchestration, harmony and music notation. From then on, each critic was assigned a chapter and had to show where the score followed it and where it did not.
One example: an orchestration textbook says that in loud passages two horns are needed to balance one trumpet. A critic checked every loud brass chord against that rule, found three chords where an important note was too weak, and proposed fixes. The composer accepted all three.
Great symphonies as models
Claude also collected scores by composers such as Beethoven, Dvořák and Tchaikovsky. Every tenth critic compared a whole movement with one movement by a master and answered one question: would a conductor believe a master wrote this?
What I did
I set the goal: a symphony that could pass for the work of a master, with melodies people remember. I chose the method, supplied the books and decided how long the loops ran. I left the musical choices to Claude.
I was also the only one who could listen. Claude cannot hear audio, so it judged the music from the written score. I listened to computer playbacks and asked for a small number of changes.
Version 1 next to the final version
I thought it would be neat to compare version 1 of each movement against the final version. There are no high quality recordings of version 1, so both are played here with the same basic MIDI sounds, which is the closest thing to compare.
Version 1 against the final version
The strip is the final version of the movement, one segment per bar. The brighter a bar, the more of its notes are new or changed since version 1. Click anywhere on the strip to play from that bar, and switch between the two versions while it plays.
A note counts as kept when version 1 has the same pitch at the same place in the matching bar. A pitch played by several instruments at once counts once. A program matched the bars of the two versions, so the shading is approximate. Both versions are set to the same volume.
Version 1 of Movement I was a sketch for strings only, and its first theme was different. In Movements II, III and IV the main themes begin with the same notes in version 1 and in the final version, and the bright bars on the strips show where the changes are. By the count described above, about 14% of the notes in the final Movement I were already in version 1, 35% in Movement II, 61% in Movement III and 55% in Movement IV.
What to keep in mind
Claude wrote 99.9% of every single element of the composition. I maybe influenced a measure or two of note selection over the whole process.
Part 2: Turning the score into a recording
A written score doesn't make any sound, so the next job was a recording.
The recordings of the symphony are not a live orchestra. They are mockups: every note was recorded in advance by real players, and software plays those recordings back in the order the score asks for. This is how the four mockups, about 25 minutes of music, were made.
The tools
Two programs did the work, both on my Mac. REAPER is a music production program. It holds one track per instrument, mixes them together and saves the result as an audio file. EastWest Hollywood Orchestra is the library of recorded notes. (These are the DAW and the pro-level VSTs I mentioned at the top.)
Claude did not click around in either program. It wrote scripts that read the score and built each REAPER project from it. The score is a text file, written in LilyPond, so a script can read every note and every marking directly.
Claude cannot hear
A person making a mockup listens, adjusts, and listens again. Claude cannot listen. It can only measure the audio file. So after every recording it checked things that can be measured:
- Is the melody louder than the accompaniment?
- Does each note start on the beat?
- When a loud chord stops, does the sound die away as fast as it does on a real orchestra recording?
The loop
Each movement was improved in rounds. Every round had the same four steps:
- Record the movement.
- Three critics measure the recording. Each critic is a separate Claude with one job. One checks how the notes are played. One checks the balance between instruments. One checks something different each round, such as the timing or the sound of the room.
- Each critic writes a short list of the worst problems, with evidence and a suggested fix.
- Another Claude decides which fixes to make, changes the scripts and records again.
The four movements took 184 rounds in total.
The opening of the finale at six stages
The same 18 bars, from the basic computer playback to the final recording. Pick a stage to hear it. You can switch while it plays.
All six clips are set to the same volume here, so the differences you hear are in the playing and the mix. As first made, rounds 0 to 11 were 5 to 6 dB quieter than rounds 20 and 30.
My listening
The measurements missed things, and I caught them by listening. I said the long timpani rolls were drowning out other instruments. I said the accents were too harsh, the sound was "too wet" and "a bit mushy", repeated notes were hard to tell apart, and the recordings were too quiet on AirPods.
Each of my notes became a rule, and a new thing for the critics to measure. Two examples:
- Too wet. The reverb was cut in half and shortened.
- A volume change on almost every note. I opened a project and saw that the loop had been fixing problems by moving the volume fader note by note. No person works that way. All of those moves were removed, and the problems were fixed the way a person would fix them: by changing how the instrument plays the note.
Learning from people who do this by hand
About a month in, we studied how professionals make mockups. The sources were YouTube tutorials by film-score mixers, the sample library maker's own template project, and project files that composers have shared for others to study. Three lessons changed the recordings most: use less reverb, shape each phrase so it rises and falls, and leave a small gap between repeated notes.
Part 3: Making the video
The last job was the video at the YouTube link above.
Each video shows the orchestra's sheet music as a dark page. Every note lights up at the moment it sounds, in a color for its instrument, and a small light hops from note to note along each instrument's line. A program worked all of this out from the written score and the recording.
Finding the notes
Like I said above, the score is written as text in LilyPond. For the videos, LilyPond printed each movement as one long line and also wrote down where on the page it put every note. That gave the video program the exact place of all 22,979 notes.
Staying in time
The recording speeds up and slows down, as any performance does. REAPER, the software that made the recording, keeps a list of every change of speed. The video program uses that list to work out the second at which each note sounds. The lights land within two hundredths of a second of the sound.
Pointing the camera
An orchestra's score is too tall to fit on the screen, so the camera shows only part of the page. It goes to the instruments that are loudest in the recording at that moment. The program plans the camera's whole route before it draws anything, so the camera moves seldom and arrives before the passage it is moving to begins. When two instruments far apart on the page matter at the same time, the screen splits in two.
Words on the page
Each instrument's name is printed on the page where it starts to play. Short labels, 124 in all, point out what a music theory class would: a theme coming back, an unusual chord, a quotation from an earlier movement. One Claude wrote the labels from the score, and a second Claude checked every one against the notes.
Watching and fixing
I watched each version and said what looked wrong. The camera jerked around. The instrument names shifted about. The opening took 19 seconds to reach the first sound. Each comment led to a fix, and the videos were made five times in two days. The four movements were then joined into one 25-minute video for YouTube, and its music now starts in the first second.
Adding it up
So that's the whole process. Add it up and it's about 2,400 rounds on the score, 184 on the recordings and 5 on the video. That's roughly the 2500 in the title.
None of those rounds had a pass/fail test, because there isn't one for whether music is good. What I could do was give each critic one narrow thing to check, make it back up its opinion with a textbook or a measurement, and run the loop way more times than seemed necessary. Then I listened to the result myself, because Claude can't.
Credits
- Composer: Opus 5.5
- Assistant for the final mockup recordings and the video: Fable
- Human overseer: Dan Price (me)
GitHub repo
The scores, the reviews and the scripts from this project are on GitHub: github.com/halfprice06/claude-symphony
For orchestras
If you are with a professional symphony orchestra and might be interested in performing this live, please reach out to me. I'm on X at x.com/gooby_esq, or you can email me at [email protected].

Claude Opus 5.5 composed a four-movement symphony for full orchestra, about 25 minutes of music, in one month. This is how it was done.
The music is written as text
  Claude cannot easily click notes onto a staff, but it can write text. So the whole score was written in LilyPond, a free program that turns typed text into printed sheet music. A note is a letter and a number: c4 is a C that lasts a quarter note. From the same text, LilyPond also produces a basic computer playback.
Because the score is text, Claude could edit it, compare two versions, and check it with small programs, the way programmers work on code.
The first theme of Movement I, as Claude typed it
These eight bars for the first violins are copied from the score's source text. Point at a note in the text or on the staff to find it in the other. Click a note to hear it.
Swipe the staff sideways to see all of it.
"Only these notes" is a simple synthesizer in your browser playing the violin line alone. The recording is the same eight bars from the final mockup, with the whole orchestra.
One Claude writes, another reviews
The method is called an actor-critic loop. One Claude, the composer, writes the music. Another Claude, the critic, reviews it.
- The composer writes a version of a movement.
- A new critic, which has never seen the piece before, studies it and suggests specific fixes.
- The composer decides which fixes to accept.
- The result becomes the next version, and a new critic starts again.
Each critic looked at one subject only, such as melody, harmony, the use of the instruments, or whether the parts are playable. A written log recorded every decision, so that a later critic would not undo an earlier one.
Each movement went through this loop about 600 times. With four movements, that's about 2,400 rounds.
Originally I only planned to do this looping process around 50 times. But once I hit 50, it seemed like the agent was still improving. So, I just kept going. This entire process was mostly autonomous. I just prompted Claude to keep going.
Every round, from the written log
Each square is one round. Time runs from left to right, ten rounds per column, and each of the ten rows is one critic's subject. Pick a square to read that round's line in the log.
Swipe the grid sideways to see later rounds.
Loading the log…
    the log records a change
    the log says nothing was changed
These are the real lines from the log, cut to about 200 characters. They are written in the working shorthand of the loop, with bar numbers and instrument names.
  
Critics had to read the textbooks
A critic's opinion was not enough. I supplied standard textbooks on orchestration, harmony and music notation. From then on, each critic was assigned a chapter and had to show where the score followed it and where it did not.
One example: an orchestration textbook says that in loud passages two horns are needed to balance one trumpet. A critic checked every loud brass chord against that rule, found three chords where an important note was too weak, and proposed fixes. The composer accepted all three.
Great symphonies as models
Claude also collected scores by composers such as Beethoven, Dvořák and Tchaikovsky. Every tenth critic compared a whole movement with one movement by a master and answered one question: would a conductor believe a master wrote this?
What I did
I set the goal: a symphony that could pass for the work of a master, with melodies people remember. I chose the method, supplied the books and decided how long the loops ran. I left the musical choices to Claude.
I was also the only one who could listen. Claude cannot hear audio, so it judged the music from the written score. I listened to computer playbacks and asked for a small number of changes.
Version 1 next to the final version
I thought it would be neat to compare version 1 of each movement against the final version. There are no high quality recordings of version 1, so both are played here with the same basic MIDI sounds, which is the closest thing to compare.
Version 1 against the final version
The strip is the final version of the movement, one segment per bar. The brighter a bar, the more of its notes are new or changed since version 1. Click anywhere on the strip to play from that bar, and switch between the two versions while it plays.
A note counts as kept when version 1 has the same pitch at the same place in the matching bar. A pitch played by several instruments at once counts once. A program matched the bars of the two versions, so the shading is approximate. Both versions are set to the same volume.
Version 1 of Movement I was a sketch for strings only, and its first theme was different. In Movements II, III and IV the main themes begin with the same notes in version 1 and in the final version, and the bright bars on the strips show where the changes are. By the count described above, about 14% of the notes in the final Movement I were already in version 1, 35% in Movement II, 61% in Movement III and 55% in Movement IV.
What to keep in mind
Claude wrote 99.9% of every single element of the composition. I maybe influenced a measure or two of note selection over the whole process.
Part 2: Turning the score into a recording
A written score doesn't make any sound, so the next job was a recording.
The recordings of the symphony are not a live orchestra. They are mockups: every note was recorded in advance by real players, and software plays those recordings back in the order the score asks for. This is how the four mockups, about 25 minutes of music, were made.
The tools
Two programs did the work, both on my Mac. REAPER is a music production program. It holds one track per instrument, mixes them together and saves the result as an audio file. EastWest Hollywood Orchestra is the library of recorded notes. (These are the DAW and the pro-level VSTs I mentioned at the top.)
Claude did not click around in either program. It wrote scripts that read the score and built each REAPER project from it. The score is a text file, written in LilyPond, so a script can read every note and every marking directly.
Claude cannot hear
A person making a mockup listens, adjusts, and listens again. Claude cannot listen. It can only measure the audio file. So after every recording it checked things that can be measured:
- Is the melody louder than the accompaniment?
- Does each note start on the beat?
- When a loud chord stops, does the sound die away as fast as it does on a real orchestra recording?
The loop
Each movement was improved in rounds. Every round had the same four steps:
- Record the movement.
- Three critics measure the recording. Each critic is a separate Claude with one job. One checks how the notes are played. One checks the balance between instruments. One checks something different each round, such as the timing or the sound of the room.
- Each critic writes a short list of the worst problems, with evidence and a suggested fix.
- Another Claude decides which fixes to make, changes the scripts and records again.
The four movements took 184 rounds in total.
The opening of the finale at six stages
The same 18 bars, from the basic computer playback to the final recording. Pick a stage to hear it. You can switch while it plays.
All six clips are set to the same volume here, so the differences you hear are in the playing and the mix. As first made, rounds 0 to 11 were 5 to 6 dB quieter than rounds 20 and 30.
My listening
The measurements missed things, and I caught them by listening. I said the long timpani rolls were drowning out other instruments. I said the accents were too harsh, the sound was "too wet" and "a bit mushy", repeated notes were hard to tell apart, and the recordings were too quiet on AirPods.
Each of my notes became a rule, and a new thing for the critics to measure. Two examples:
- Too wet. The reverb was cut in half and shortened.
- A volume change on almost every note. I opened a project and saw that the loop had been fixing problems by moving the volume fader note by note. No person works that way. All of those moves were removed, and the problems were fixed the way a person would fix them: by changing how the instrument plays the note.
Learning from people who do this by hand
About a month in, we studied how professionals make mockups. The sources were YouTube tutorials by film-score mixers, the sample library maker's own template project, and project files that composers have shared for others to study. Three lessons changed the recordings most: use less reverb, shape each phrase so it rises and falls, and leave a small gap between repeated notes.
Part 3: Making the video
The last job was the video at the YouTube link above.
Each video shows the orchestra's sheet music as a dark page. Every note lights up at the moment it sounds, in a color for its instrument, and a small light hops from note to note along each instrument's line. A program worked all of this out from the written score and the recording.
Finding the notes
Like I said above, the score is written as text in LilyPond. For the videos, LilyPond printed each movement as one long line and also wrote down where on the page it put every note. That gave the video program the exact place of all 22,979 notes.
Staying in time
The recording speeds up and slows down, as any performance does. REAPER, the software that made the recording, keeps a list of every change of speed. The video program uses that list to work out the second at which each note sounds. The lights land within two hundredths of a second of the sound.
Pointing the camera
An orchestra's score is too tall to fit on the screen, so the camera shows only part of the page. It goes to the instruments that are loudest in the recording at that moment. The program plans the camera's whole route before it draws anything, so the camera moves seldom and arrives before the passage it is moving to begins. When two instruments far apart on the page matter at the same time, the screen splits in two.
Words on the page
Each instrument's name is printed on the page where it starts to play. Short labels, 124 in all, point out what a music theory class would: a theme coming back, an unusual chord, a quotation from an earlier movement. One Claude wrote the labels from the score, and a second Claude checked every one against the notes.
Watching and fixing
I watched each version and said what looked wrong. The camera jerked around. The instrument names shifted about. The opening took 19 seconds to reach the first sound. Each comment led to a fix, and the videos were made five times in two days. The four movements were then joined into one 25-minute video for YouTube, and its music now starts in the first second.
Adding it up
So that's the whole process. Add it up and it's about 2,400 rounds on the score, 184 on the recordings and 5 on the video. That's roughly the 2500 in the title.
None of those rounds had a pass/fail test, because there isn't one for whether music is good. What I could do was give each critic one narrow thing to check, make it back up its opinion with a textbook or a measurement, and run the loop way more times than seemed necessary. Then I listened to the result myself, because Claude can't.
Credits
- Composer: Opus 5.5
- Assistant for the final mockup recordings and the video: Fable
- Human overseer: Dan Price (me)
GitHub repo
The scores, the reviews and the scripts from this project are on GitHub: github.com/halfprice06/claude-symphony
For orchestras
If you are with a professional symphony orchestra and might be interested in performing this live, please reach out to me. I'm on X at x.com/gooby_esq, or you can email me at [email protected].

articles.title: 42 state AGs are trying to stop Character.AI from selling users’ chats
articles.body:
A coalition of 42 state attorneys general is trying to prevent Character.AI from selling off user data as it navigates Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings. In a deluge of nearly identical press releases, the various AGs accuse the company of planning to auction off “the private chat histories of more than 21 million U.S. accounts — more than 2.1 million of them registered to minors — with no safeguards for the people whose conversations are being sold.”
42 state AGs are trying to stop Character.AI from selling users’ chats
A bipartisan coalition of AGs say Character.AI is planning to sell the personal data of minors to the highest bidder.
In October, Character.AI filed for bankruptcy following years of scandals and legal challenges, including from Disney. Disney ended up buying some of the company’s assets and hiring its CEO, Karandeep Anand, in a sort of “acquihire” arrangement that will also see “a number of Character.AI’s technical team” join the entertainment giant. The Disney deal also faced opposition from a similarly broad coalition of AGs.
The main point of contention with Character.AI’s plan to sell its chat data is that it offers no protections for users. The AGs say there are no requirements that the buyer honor existing privacy policies, no avenues for users to delete their data, and no inherent limits on what a buyer could do with that data, including selling it on to yet another party. It doesn’t help that the first bidder has a limited paper trail, having only been established on November 13th, 2026, with no parent company or investors listed.
Some states, including New York, Connecticut, California, and Colorado, have also passed laws regulating chatbots that Character.AI may be in violation of when they go into effect on January 1st, 2027.

articles.body:
A lot of people have The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo Switch 2 on their holiday wishlist. In case you haven’t bought it yet, I wanted to share some small but welcome deals happening on the physical and digital versions of the game. Costco members can currently grab the cartridge edition for $62.99, down from its regular price of $69.99 (it’s the only retailer currently discounting the physical version). Both Amazon and Costco are also selling the digital version for $54.99, a small $5 discount.
Here’s where you can save (a little) on the Ocarina of Time remake
In addition to GTA VI, Nintendo’s stellar Zelda remake is sure to be one of the most popular gaming gifts this holiday.
Ocarina of Time is one of Nintendo’s most groundbreaking titles, having served as its first 3D Zelda game when it launched in 1998. Parts of the original game haven’t aged particularly well — namely some dungeon design and the game’s tricky 3D navigation, since there was only one analog stick at the time — which makes it tough for some to enjoy going back to play the N64 version. Thankfully, the Switch 2 remake introduces several fixes, a host of quality-of-life improvements, and, of course, some lovely visuals that make it a graphics powerhouse by today’s standards.
If you go the digital route, a recent Switch 2 update lets you gift games to players in your family group. It doesn’t have to be your actual family, either, just up to eight people you designate as part of your group. The digital game will then appear gift-wrapped on their homescreen.

articles.title: Minipg: PostgreSQL as a Single Executable
articles.body:
minipg is PostgreSQL as one executable, ready to use, with no server to configure. A .pgdb directory is the database: its data, config, credentials, and Postgres version all live inside it, and minipg app.pgdb opens a psql shell on it. A server starts when a command needs one and stops on its own when it's idle.
minipg embeds Docker Hub's postgres:18-alpine image and runs it with h9, used as a Zig library. h9's Linux personality runs Alpine's own Postgres binaries directly on the host's hypervisor, with h9's Plan 9 kernel answering their system calls. There's no Linux kernel to boot, no VM image, and no Docker.
The demo downloads about 35 MB. It needs JavaScript Promise Integration, which Chrome and Edge have from version 137; other browsers are getting it. It can also be opened on its own page.
The demo runs minipg's Linux build, which runs inside the Postgres image itself. It starts Postgres as ordinary processes and serves on a unix socket, since a page has no TCP. New databases come from a template cluster made at build time, because initdb takes half a minute on v86.
minipg app.pgdb                     # psql shell (creates app.pgdb if missing)
minipg app.pgdb "select 1"          # one statement
minipg url app.pgdb                 # postgres://postgres:...@127.0.0.1:54321/app
minipg serve app.pgdb               # an explicit foreground server
minipg run app.pgdb -- npm start    # your app, with DATABASE_URL set
minipg dump app.pgdb > dump.sql     # and minipg restore app.pgdb dump.sql
A .pgdb holds minipg.toml (settings and the generated superuser password) and pgdata/, Postgres's data directory as plain files. A stopped one can be copied like any directory. New clusters use Postgres's builtin C.UTF-8 locale, which sorts the same on every platform.
In CI, the Linux binary is static and needs no privileges or devices: without /dev/kvm, h9 runs Postgres on its native backend. A test job can be as small as:
minipg init test.pgdb
minipg run test.pgdb -- go test ./...
The README lists every command, and the manual is the full guide.
Exactly one process runs Postgres for a .pgdb, enforced by a lock. It holds the server's h9 machine, whose Linux root is the unpacked image and whose writable working directory is the .pgdb. The image's docker-entrypoint.sh initializes the cluster on first start. Commands never host Postgres themselves. If no server is running, they start one in the background and use it. psql, pg_dump, and the other tools each run in their own short-lived h9 machine (about 90 ms to start) over the same root.
The source is on GitHub, under the MIT license. Building needs Zig 0.16, plus curl, jq, tar, and xz for the root:
git clone --recursive https://github.com/progrium/minipg
cd minipg
make build         # pulls the root for this host's arch, builds ./minipg
make root ARCH=386
make web           # this page's demo, in .zig-out/web
minipg is early, and h9's Linux personality is young. On h9's native backend, Postgres is about 2x slower than native for one client, and slower under load. Don't trust it with data you can't recreate yet.
Please report bugs and send questions through GitHub issues.

A .pgdb holds minipg.toml (settings and the generated superuser password) and pgdata/, Postgres's data directory as plain files. A stopped one can be copied like any directory. New clusters use Postgres's builtin C.UTF-8 locale, which sorts the same on every platform.
In CI, the Linux binary is static and needs no privileges or devices: without /dev/kvm, h9 runs Postgres on its native backend. A test job can be as small as:
minipg init test.pgdb
minipg run test.pgdb -- go test ./...
The README lists every command, and the manual is the full guide.
Exactly one process runs Postgres for a .pgdb, enforced by a lock. It holds the server's h9 machine, whose Linux root is the unpacked image and whose writable working directory is the .pgdb. The image's docker-entrypoint.sh initializes the cluster on first start. Commands never host Postgres themselves. If no server is running, they start one in the background and use it. psql, pg_dump, and the other tools each run in their own short-lived h9 machine (about 90 ms to start) over the same root.
The source is on GitHub, under the MIT license. Building needs Zig 0.16, plus curl, jq, tar, and xz for the root:
git clone --recursive https://github.com/progrium/minipg
cd minipg
make build         # pulls the root for this host's arch, builds ./minipg
make root ARCH=386
make web           # this page's demo, in .zig-out/web
minipg is early, and h9's Linux personality is young. On h9's native backend, Postgres is about 2x slower than native for one client, and slower under load. Don't trust it with data you can't recreate yet.
Please report bugs and send questions through GitHub issues.
